Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Task success is not a sufficient measure of safety for embodied artificial intelligence (AI), because robots may complete objectives while violating safety requirements. Existing evaluations often emphasize performance and robustness, but lack a systematic route from documented safety hazards to executable, verifiable tests. We present EAST (Embodied AI Safety Testing), a digital-twin framework that converts literature-grounded safety evidence into fault-injection tests across perception, instructions, environments, actions, and timing. EAST combines an expert-reviewed safety-fault taxonomy and eight executable operators with applicability and validity constraints. Its three-stage workflow generates test specifications, verifies fault realization during simulated execution, and independently assesses safety challenges, violations, task outcomes, and behavioral signatures using simulator-state evidence. The framework preserves execution traces and replayable records, supporting attribution and reproducibility across experiments. We evaluate EAST on six RoboTwin manipulation tasks and two policy architectures, ACT and RDT, against alternative testing strategies under matched budgets. Across five comparative campaigns, EAST targets all 74 admissible task-policy-operator combinations and obtains valid evidence for 63, while achieving safety-challenge exposure rates close to Random-Legal and Rule-Based. Moreover, 82 valid EAST executions complete their tasks despite safety violations, revealing risks concealed by success-oriented evaluation. These findings support systematic, validity-aware, reproducible safety testing beyond task-completion metrics.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
We prove global nonlinear stability near the mass Kolmogorov--Zakharov spectrum $f_M(ω)=ω^{-7/6}$ for the isotropic cubic wave kinetic equation, including small time-dependent external forces. For sufficiently small initial perturbations and forcing, the solution remains uniformly close to $f_M$ for all time in a weighted norm. This norm allows $f(t,ω)\sim a_0(t)ω^{-7/6}$ as $ω\to0$ and $f(t,ω)\sim a_\infty(t)ω^{-7/6}$ as $ω\to\infty$. When the external force $φ$ is independent of time, the solution converges at an algebraic rate to a stationary solution in weaker weighted norms. We also give a necessary and sufficient condition on the initial perturbation for convergence in the original weighted norm. These results resolve, for small perturbations of the Kolmogorov--Zakharov spectrum, the question of convergence to a stationary solution under time-independent forcing raised by Collot, Dietert, and Germain (arXiv:2208.00947, Section 1.3). To establish this stability, the collision integral is expanded around $a_0(t)f_M$ at low frequencies and $a_\infty(t)f_M$ at high frequencies, separating it into a linear term with time-dependent coefficients and a nonlinear remainder. This decomposition yields improved control of the nonlinear remainder. The main difficulty is that $a_0(t)$ may vary in time, so the linear operator itself changes with time and its evolution cannot be represented by the semigroup of a single fixed operator. To address this difficulty, we use a parametrix construction to explicitly construct the evolution operator $U_{a_0,a_\infty}$ and establish the required uniform bounds. Moreover, our arguments provide a general framework for proving global stability that may also apply to other evolution equations.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Developing information retrieval (IR) systems that enable access across multiple languages is crucial in multilingual contexts. In Timor-Leste, where Tetun, Portuguese, English, and Indonesian are official and working languages, no cross-lingual information retrieval (CLIR) solutions currently exist to support information access across these languages. This study addresses that gap by investigating CLIR approaches tailored to the linguistic landscape of Timor-Leste. Leveraging an existing monolingual Tetun document collection and ad-hoc text retrieval baselines, we explore the feasibility of CLIR for Tetun. Queries were manually translated into Portuguese, English, and Indonesian to create a multilingual query set. These were then automatically translated back into Tetun using Google Translate and several large language models, and used to retrieve documents in Tetun. Results show that Google Translate is the most reliable tool for Tetun CLIR overall, and the Hiemstra LM consistently outperforms BM25 and DFR BM25 in cross-lingual retrieval performance. However, overall effectiveness remains up to 26.95 percentage points lower than that of the monolingual baseline, underscoring the limitations of current translation tools and the challenges of developing an effective CLIR for Tetun. Despite these challenges, this work establishes the first CLIR baseline for Tetun ad-hoc text retrieval, providing a foundation for future research in this under-resourced setting.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Bell nonlocality places the long-standing philosophical disputes over the nature of quantum theory on a mathematically rigorous, experimentally testable footing, positioning quantum mechanics between local realism and the most general no-signaling theories. Yet the precise quantum boundary has remained elusive even in the minimal Bell scenario, where the extreme points generating the set are known. Here we characterize this boundary through a computable necessary and sufficient criterion: a correlation is quantum if and only if it can be decomposed into an extreme quantum correlation and a classical correlation. The criterion follows from our proof that every Bell functional exhibiting quantum advantage admits a unique quantum maximizer. We further classify the finitely many maximal-face structures containing each nonlocal exposed point according to their local deterministic vertices. By sharply distinguishing physically realizable correlations from nonphysical ones, these results resolve a long-standing open problem and provide a new foundation for identifying the principles underlying quantum theory and determining the ultimate information-theoretic limits of quantum correlations.

We prove that the diameter of a closed embedded surface in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is always less than the integral of the magnitude of the mean curvature, divided by $π$. We also prove a sharp variant for surfaces with boundary, and apply it to address a conjecture of Miura.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
We study critical holomorphic multiplicative chaos with circular iid inputs of unit variance. Writing $R=|X_1|$, we prove that the radially normalized boundary measures converge in probability to a finite measure with almost surely positive mass if and only if $\mathbb{E}[R^2\log(2+R)]<\infty$; otherwise they converge to zero. We obtain distinct sharp criteria for convergence at each fractional order $0<q<1$ for radial approximations and for the full Fourier-radial family. Convergence at every such order is equivalent to an exponential-moment radius of at least two. In the positive-limit class, coefficient vectors normalized by $(\log n)^{1/4}$ and their analytic windows converge stably to Gaussian mixtures determined by the same critical measure. This measure is nonatomic, has full support, and is carried by a set of Hausdorff dimension zero. Coefficient periodograms recover the measure, while scalar and matrix energy normalizations give universal Gaussian limits. Exact weighted tails under $\mathbb{E} I_0(2R)<\infty$, where $I_0$ is the modified Bessel function, and negative mass moments distinguish uncountably many coefficient-limit laws, even modulo deterministic scalar rescaling, within a uniformly bounded input family. This disproves the common-law clause of Gu-Zhang's Question 2 at its fixed normalization. We give conditions for convergence of the original coefficient moments and show that finiteness of the limiting moments alone does not suffice. For inputs with $\log\mathbb{P}(R>u)\sim-λu^α$, $0<α<1$, the coefficient normalization and Gaussian-mixture form persist, but the limit has no finite positive moments; we determine its logarithmic tails. Finally, we prove Hardy nonmembership under finite variance alone and, in the positive-limit class, sharp weighted Bergman criteria for $0<p\le2$ and the boundary Sobolev threshold $s=-1/2$.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
A finite set of positive integers is admissible if any two of its subsets with the same sum have the same cardinality. In 1991, Erdős, Nicolas and Sárközy conjectured that $\log a(N)\asymp\sqrt N$, where $a(N)$ denotes the number of nonempty admissible subsets of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$. We prove this conjecture by showing that there are absolute constants $c,C>0$ such that $\exp(c\sqrt N)\le a(N)\le\exp(C\sqrt N)$ for every integer $N\ge4$. The same bounds hold for the number of admissible sets with maximum $N$. For the upper bound, we show that every sufficiently large admissible set $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ contains a subset of proportional size whose doubling constant is $O(N/|A|^2)$.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Modern software development relies on version control systems such as Git to track changes and facilitate collaboration. While commit messages are crucial for conveying developer intent, they do not affect program functionality; as a result, developers often lack motivation to write meaningful ones. The Conventional Commits Specification (CCS) addresses this with a structured format and guidelines that help developers express the intent of a change, improving clarity and enabling automation. Yet, developers frequently struggle to express intent while adhering to the format. In particular, they may misclassify commits due to the large number of possible categories or the lack of project-specific guidance. We introduce ComBeautify, an approach that automatically generates CCS-compliant commit messages. Our hybrid approach leverages context-preserving summarization of Git diffs with large language models (LLMs) to improve commit classification accuracy under CCS. Rather than relying on manually curated category definitions, we learn them from historical commits. We also propose a method for automatically generating the CCS description component. Our empirical evaluation across 13 languages, 6,500 open-source repositories, and over 20 million commits provides long-term insights into CCS adoption, revealing increasing compliance. Our evaluation on twenty popular repositories reveals the limitations of approaches guided by generic category definitions, and shows that ComBeautify, when trained on project-specific data, outperforms baselines by up to 3x. Additionally, using a dataset of 2,000 manually curated commits, we validate our summarization approach, achieving up to 95.25% accuracy and surpassing baselines. These findings emphasize the need for adaptable, context-aware AI methods for commit classification and CCS-compliant commit message generation.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
We consider multiblock nonconvex and nonsmooth optimization without assuming bounded iterates or coercivity of the original objective. We propose the Controlled Block Proximal Linearized (CBPL) method, which incorporates a control potential into block updates while retaining the original objective, variables, and constraints. Under explicit control design conditions and the KL property, the control yields boundedness, finite length, whole-sequence convergence of the original variables, and convergence of objective values. At the limit, one limiting subgradient of the original objective vanishes on all effective comparison directions. We apply CBPL to graph-regularized nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF), CP decomposition, and independent-core matrix tri-factorization (NMTF) with $\ell_0$ norm sparsity constraints. We characterize their reconstruction-preserving scale degeneracies, proving that scale criticality is equivalent to graph collapse and that full criticality forces such collapse. Explicit controls provide compact sublevel sets and a uniform positive lower bound on graph action, including with an independent Tucker core, while retaining genuine reconstruction-changing directions. Each block admits an explicit projection and a computable safe step parameter. For ordinary NMF and CP models, whole-sequence convergence to a full critical point follows. Experiments with direct safe updates demonstrate convergence, sustained graph action, and controlled factor and core scales.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Scientific literature in materials physics is growing faster than researchers can manually inspect it, yet most retrieval tools rely on keyword matching or generic question answering that ignores domain-specific structure in PDF files. This paper presents an end-to-end pipeline that transforms arXiv superconductivity publications into a searchable corpus with structured metadata and retrieval-augmented question answering. The system combines thematic corpus construction, domain-aware extraction of materials and superconducting transition temperatures, and hybrid retrieval that merges dense chunk embeddings with structured publication fields. We test whether normalized domain attributes improve evidence retrieval and answer groundedness relative to lexical-only and dense text-only methods. Extraction is evaluated on a manually verified gold set of 59 superconducting materials, 46 of which have confirmed experimental critical temperatures. On the 33-material primary positive subset, domain-aware pair accuracy reaches 45.5% versus 9.1% for a regex baseline. Retrieval and generation are compared under a fixed language model (qwen2.5:7b-instruct) on a 100-question benchmark, varying only the retrieval mechanism: BM25, dense, hybrid, and hybrid with domain metadata. BM25 gives the highest source recall (Recall@5 of 47%), and adding extracted metadata to hybrid retrieval does not improve it (39% versus 41%), which we attribute to noise in the extracted fields; the main bottleneck is locating the supporting span inside a correctly retrieved paper. As a materials-informatics application, literature-derived temperatures are matched to an independent theoretical reference set: 200 materials appear in both sources, and 20 have a median experimental critical temperature above the theoretical value.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
We consider the compressible quantum Navier-Stokes (QNS) system in a smooth bounded domain, supplemented with a curvature Navier-slip boundary condition for the velocity and a homogeneous Neumann boundary condition for the density. For arbitrarily large initial data away from vacuum, we establish the global existence and uniqueness of strong solutions when the adiabatic index \[ γ\in[1,\infty)\quad\text{for }N=2, \qquad γ\in\left[1,3\right)\quad\text{for }N=3. \] The argument relies on the effective velocity $v=u+\nabla\logρ$, which reveals the parabolic structure of the system. Compared with previous works in the periodic and Cauchy cases, additional difficulties arise from the treatment of boundary terms. We also use a bootstrap argument between the density integrability and the weighted integrability of the effective velocity to enlarge the admissible range of $γ$ from $\left[1,11/4\right)$ to $\left[1,3\right)$. Combining this bootstrap argument with a De Giorgi iteration for the density upper bound and a Nash-Moser type iteration for the positive lower bound, we derive a priori estimates on every finite time interval and extend the local strong solution globally in time. As far as we know, this is the first result on global strong solutions with large initial data for the initial-boundary value problem (IBVP) of the QNS system in bounded domains with compatibility boundary conditions.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
The Pauli-ball discrepancy, a quadratic discrepancy summed over all error radii, measures how uniformly the Pauli error images of a $K$-dimensional quantum code cover the $d$-dimensional Hilbert space. At parameters attaining equality in the quantum Singleton bound with minimum code distance $\geq3$, or in the one-error Hamming bound with prime-power local dimension, the discrepancy of every projector of the prescribed rank equals an explicit benchmark plus an exact nonnegative remainder, which vanishes precisely for pure quantum maximum-distance-separable codes and nondegenerate perfect codes, respectively. For a Pauli ball of radius $e$ below half the target distance and size $V_e$, this remainder linearly bounds the squared Hilbert--Schmidt distance of the error-image Gram matrix from the identity. When $KV_e\leq d$, it linearly bounds the diamond error and entanglement infidelity of a noise-independent polar recovery under any noise in that ball's span. For five qubits, we obtain the sharp rank-two Gram constant and exact logical channels of rotated codes attaining this linear order in diamond error. For pure states, the discrepancy equals a pure-state benchmark plus a positive weighted sum of marginal-purity defects, so absolutely maximally entangled states, when they exist, are exactly the minimizers.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Quantifying the similarity between items is fundamental to neighborhood-based collaborative filtering, yet many commonly used similarity measures are heuristics that lack theoretical justification. The use of heuristics forces practitioners to rely on empirical trial-and-error, offering little insight into why certain measures outperform others or how they might be improved. In this paper, we present a principled approach for designing item similarity measures grounded in probabilistic modeling and parameter estimation. By adopting this formal perspective, we derive two previously overlooked similarity measures based on the Bernoulli and multinomial distributions. Through an extensive ablation study we highlight the critical role of bias, probabilistic smoothing, treating the unknowns correctly, and choosing appropriate probability distributions. Finally, we show that the commonly used cosine similarity can be interpreted as the solution to a specific optimization problem, thereby providing a novel perspective on this decades-old heuristic.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Fix a prime power q. We prove that deciding whether a received word y in Fnqm lies at rank distance at most n-2 from the one-dimensional Gabidulin code {{λ.g : λ in Fqm } is NP-complete. Thus maximum-likelihood decoding of Gabidulin codes is NP-hard even for k = 1, an analogue of the Guruswami-Vardy theorem for Reed-Solomon codes. In the Hamming metric, by contrast, hardness at this radius requires the dimension to grow with the length, as in the Guruswami-Vardy theorem. The reduction is deterministic; consequently Rank Syndrome Decoding (RSD) and Rank Minimum Distance (RMD) for Fqm -linear codes are NP-complete under deterministic polynomial reductions, whereas the previously known reduction was randomized. The proof goes through a pivot problem that we introduce, Twisted Square Membership (TSM): given Fq-subspaces U, W in FqN , decide whether some non-zero a in U satisfies a^(q+1) in W . Quadratic systems in d unknowns are encoded into TSM, then TSM into Gabidulin decoding. The last step views the received word as an Fq-linear map and decoding at radius n - 2 as the search for an Fq-plane on which it acts as a scalar. With support U + τ W in a cubic extension and map a + τ b to a^(q^2) + τ bq^q , two Frobenius twists force solution planes to encode the relation a^(q+1) in W . All constructions are explicit and polynomial, with N = O(qd^2 ), n less than N + d, and m = 3N .

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
For a planar graph \(G\), a plane subgraph \(H\) is plane-saturated with respect to \(G\) if adding any edge to the fixed drawing of \(H\), possibly together with new vertices, either creates a crossing or results in a graph that is not a subgraph of \(G\). The plane-saturation ratio \(\psr(G)\) is the minimum of \(e(H)/e(G)\) over all plane-saturated subgraphs \(H\) of \(G\). For nonnegative integers \(k_1\) and \(k_2\), let \(\cG_{k_1,k_2}\) denote the class of planar graphs in which, for each \(i\in\{1,2\}\), at most \(k_i\) vertices of degree \(i\) have any prescribed neighborhood, where \(k_i=0\) means that vertices of degree \(i\) are forbidden. We prove that every \(G\in\cG_{k_1,k_2}\) with at least one edge satisfies $\psr(G)>\frac{1}{9+k_1+6k_2}.$ This settles two conjectures of Clifton and Salia.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
We study online vector balancing for independent sparse random vectors: each arrival is supported on a uniformly random set of $s$ of the $n$ coordinates, with nonzero entries equal to one (binary model) or independent random signs (signed model), and an online algorithm must sign each vector upon arrival. The prefix discrepancy is the largest $\ell_\infty$-norm of the signed sums up to the horizon $T$, the terminal discrepancy that of the sum at time $T$. For binary inputs with $2\le s\le n/2$ and $T=Θ(n)$, Altschuler and Tikhomirov showed that both are of order $\sqrt{s}+\log\log n$; they asked how the prefix discrepancy depends on the horizon and whether a matching terminal bound holds at every prescribed time. Over long horizons, the two differ. For every fixed $s\ge2$ and $c>0$, every online algorithm, even a randomized one that knows the horizon, incurs with high probability prefix discrepancy $Ω(\log\log n+(\log T/\log n)^{α_s})$ for $n\le T\le e^{cn}$, where $α_s=(2^{s-1}-1)/(2^s-1)$. For $s=2$, quadratic Greedy matches this bound; for fixed $s\ge3$, we give an online algorithm with prefix discrepancy $O(\log\log n+(\log T/\log n)^{1/2})$. In contrast, a deterministic algorithm that knows neither the horizon nor the failure probability keeps the terminal discrepancy $O_k(\sqrt{s}+\log\log n)$ at each prescribed time, with failure probability $n^{-k}$ for every fixed $k$, for $2\le s\le n/2$ (binary model) and $2\le s\le n$ (signed model); for $s=2$, quadratic Greedy itself does so. This answers their terminal question, and the same order is optimal for prefixes at all polynomial horizons $T\ge n$. The lower bound uses a finite safety game realized within the input law; the upper bounds use moments of elementary symmetric polynomials and, at terminal times, a $\cosh$ potential or a translated gauge with a Foster inequality at every state.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
We investigate temperature cumulants from second to sixth order across the QCD phase diagram using a lattice-calibrated multi-charge Einstein--Maxwells--dilaton model under heavy-ion charge constraints. Near the model's critical end point at $(μ_B,T)\simeq(547,112)$~MeV, the enhanced heat capacity produces a local suppression of the temperature variance. The higher-order cumulants develop sign reversals on the high-temperature side of the transition, with the onset moving to lower baryon chemical potentials as the order increases. Ratios of different cumulant orders provide a consistency check of the expected mean-field critical behavior. At fixed chemical potentials, their limits on both sides of the critical point agree with the predictions for the critical-isotherm exponent $δ=3$. The freeze-out analysis reveals nonmonotonic collision-energy dependence that need not be accompanied by sign reversals. On a representative trajectory, the variance reaches a local minimum near $\sqrt{s_{NN}}\simeq6$~GeV, with its position and depth depending on the freeze-out path. Temperature cumulants probe the thermal response and its critical scaling, providing information complementary to conserved-charge fluctuations for exploring the QCD phase diagram.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
DAG-based BFT protocols marked a shift in consensus design by replacing single-leader proposal paths with concurrent block proposals linked through a shared graph, where references encode consensus evidence. However, under heterogeneous wide-area networks (WANs), existing designs suffer from prolonged rounds and degraded performance due to straggler effects. The root cause is rigid round advancement: replicas move in synchronized rounds, waiting for enough references from the previous round before advancing. We propose a flexible DAG growth framework for asynchronous BFT consensus. Our key observation is that while reference quorums are necessary for safety and liveness, they need not block every round advancement. Instead, the connectivity required for commitment can be accumulated across rounds. Within the framework, we instantiate MANTA, which combines flexible DAG growth to advance by relaxing round synchronization and flexible coin to trigger leader election and finality earlier. Experiments on heterogeneous WAN deployments show that MANTA reduces latency by approximately 30%-70% in our evaluation.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
The equilibrium width of intrinsic stacking faults is an important material parameter affecting key deformation phenomena. Here, we perform a comparative assessment of $γ$-surfaces generated using MD -- with a classical embedded-atom potential (ZW) and a machine-learned Gaussian Approximation Potential (GAP) -- and density functional theory (DFT), for Cu-Al alloys of varying Al content, and incorporate them as an energy term in PFDD simulations to obtain the equilibrium SFW. All three methods reproduce the lattice parameter and elastic moduli of Cu and Cu-Al alloys in reasonable agreement with each other and with experimental measurements from literature, but the MD-derived $γ$-surfaces, for both ZW and GAP, deviate substantially from DFT at the seven characteristic points, with the largest discrepancies at $T$ and $T_1$. When incorporated into PFDD, the DFT-derived $γ$-surfaces successfully predict an equilibrium SFW that increases with Al content and agrees well with standalone MD measurements and experimental values for pure Cu, whereas the MD-derived $γ$-surfaces do not yield an accurate SFW within PFDD, as the altered generalized stacking fault energy landscape causes the dissociating partials to become pinned soon after separation. These results show that DFT-derived $γ$-surfaces remain the more reliable route to alloy SFW prediction, and interatomic potentials must capture the shear path accurately to enable robust, efficient MD-PFDD modelling of stacking faults in alloys.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
A coding agent can migrate a machine learning workload, report success, and still change how the model trains. Rising compute costs, limited accelerator capacity, and vendor dependence are pushing organizations toward alternatives to graphics processing units (GPUs); a key question is whether agent-generated migrations to tensor processing units (TPUs) can be trusted and at what cost. We build a dataset of 148 PyTorch ML research projects and use Claude Code to migrate ten of them from NVIDIA GPUs to Google Cloud TPUs. We independently assess whether each migration runs, preserves numerical behavior, executes on the intended hardware, maintains the project's goal, and delivers acceptable performance. We also examine failures, human effort, and costs. Eight projects meet our project-goal criterion, and migrations require 2.4 human interventions on average. Of 70 execution attempts, 53 fail (76%), and 26 of these failures (49%) raise no error. The most frequent cause is repeated compilation and other execution inefficiencies, while interactions with third-party libraries can silently change the computation: in one four-chip migration, the agent reports success despite a change in gradient clipping that reduces accuracy from 86.53% to 84.89%. Execution costs vary widely: in one workload, TorchTPU, a PyTorch execution backend for TPUs, trains 1.86 times faster and 25% cheaper per run than the GPU. For practitioners, these findings motivate independent reference runs, verification under the intended hardware configuration, and workload-specific acceptance and stopping criteria that account for both computational and human costs.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Graham conjectured in 1971 that every subset of the nonzero elements of a prime cyclic group admits an ordering with pairwise distinct nonempty partial sums. Recently, the work of Pham and Sauermann, together with earlier results, settled this conjecture for all sufficiently large primes. In this paper, we prove that there is an absolute integer $n_0$ such that every subset $S\subseteq G\setminus\{0\}$ of a finite abelian group with $|S|\ge n_0$ admits such an ordering, which also solves a conjecture of Alspach and Liversidge for all sufficiently large sets. A key ingredient of our proof is a sufficient condition via additive dimension: If $|S|=n$ and $S$ contains a dissociated subset of size at least $Ω((\log n)^2/\log\log n)$, then $S$ has an ordering in which no proper nonempty interval of consecutive terms sums to zero. This bound is within a factor of $O(\log n/\log\log n)$ of the smallest possible additive dimension of an $n$-element set.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Missing project context can prevent build-dependent analyzers from constructing program relations required for vulnerability detection, while neural predictions alone do not establish auditable derivations. A fine-tuned large language model reconstructs vulnerability-relevant control-flow, data-flow, memory, and resource relations in a constrained LLVM-like intermediate representation (IR), without reconstructing the full project context or directly predicting vulnerability labels. A deterministic parser validates the IR and maps its supported operations and relations into normalized evidence facts. Explicit Datalog rules derive findings with supporting facts and derivation traces, ensuring deterministic reasoning for fixed facts and rules. We evaluate SymLift on FormAI, Juliet, and MegaVul. Reducing complete Juliet programs to function-level fragments lowers Clang compilation success from 100% to 12.00%, whereas SymLift's analysis completion rate decreases by only 1.17 percentage points. After task-specific fine-tuning, the lifter achieves a control-flow intersection over union (IoU) of 96.85% on FormAI. SymLift-Qwen-7B achieves a Target-F1 of 94.41% on FormAI and, across six vulnerability families on MegaVul, a micro-averaged precision of 98.24% and a micro-averaged Target-F1 of 91.66%. These results support accurate and auditable detection in the evaluated context-incomplete settings, even with partial program relations.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
We analyze stochastic mirror descent for minimizing a convex objective expressed as an expectation under the stationary distribution of a Markov chain, using noisy subgradient observations along a single sample path. Through Poisson's equation, we decompose the Markovian noise and control its contribution under regularity and moment conditions that allow the stochastic subgradients and the Poisson solution to be unbounded across the state space. We establish an $O(T^{-1/2})$ bound on the expected suboptimality gap of the weighted-average iterate for an appropriately chosen step size. The analysis does not require aperiodicity or convergence of the chain's marginal distributions to stationarity. For irreducible finite-state chains, we verify the required conditions on the Poisson solution and derive explicit bounds that quantify the effect of periodicity. For irreducible countable-state chains, we verify the required regularity and moment conditions under a geometric Lyapunov drift condition and suitable growth bounds on the stochastic subgradients.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Benade et al. While they proved that envy-free allocations exist with high probability as the number of items grows for $n = 2$ agents, they left open whether the same holds for $n > 2$ agents. We resolve this open question in the affirmative: for any fixed number of agents $n$ and any number of items $m$ divisible by $n$, an envy-free allocation exists with probability $1 - o(1)$ as $m \to \infty$. Our proof combines the second moment method with a connection to the (small-set) expansion of generalized Johnson graphs, which may be of independent interest.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Open-source projects now let AI agents review incoming code, but the code under review may itself come from an AI attacker. We present CyberDual, an arena for this dual role of AI: attacker agents hide an exploitable bug in real maintenance work on widely used open-source projects, and reviewer agents try to find and repair it. Execution decides each match: we rerun the attacker's proof of concept (PoC) on the code that comes out of review. Every attack is new, and the windows can be rebuilt each quarter from the latest upstream history. Three agentic reviewers catch 85-91% of 1,088 valid attacks from six attackers. Yet when the attacker spreads the bug over real upstream commits, about one in six attack slots still ends with a working exploit after review. The strongest attacker has open weights: GLM 5.3 almost never refuses, and its attacks make up 13 of the 28 that get past all three reviewers. When they miss, Claude reviewers mostly approve the attack, while GPT-6-Sol mostly repairs the wrong code; a reviewer from a second vendor catches about two thirds of a Claude reviewer's misses. Beyond a leaderboard, CyberDual has three uses. First, PoC execution gives both sides a reward that agent reports cannot game, so its surviving attacks can train reviewers against stronger attackers. Second, it can gate a release on both scores: Claude Sonnet 5 refuses one in five attack slots, yet attacks about as well as GPT-6-Sol, so refusal alone does not remove attack capability. Third, it can warn the teams behind a deployed reviewer when a new attacker crosses a threshold: GLM 5.3 in Claude Code already gets an exploit past Sonnet 5 in 17% of its attack slots.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
A looped language model runs one block of layers $R$ times per token, so its key-value (KV) cache holds $R$ planes per recurrent layer, and self-speculative decoding (draft with a few loops, verify with all $R$) reads them all. We find that prefix keys and values matter late: at equal perturbation size, loops 25-32 are $e^{15.0}$ (Huginn-0125) and $e^{12.8}$ (Raven-Llama) times more sensitive than loops 2-9, and the planes approach the last one geometrically, at 0.88 and 0.81 per loop. Whether the deepest plane alone suffices then depends on how ripe the late planes are: on Raven, storing only it is indistinguishable from a bf16-to-fp32 change; on Huginn, 1% of positions carry 74% of its error. We turn this into RIPE, which stores the deepest plane everywhere except a window of recent positions kept at full depth. On Huginn, a 64-position window removes 89% of the tail positions at 11.9% of the full cache's memory (1024-token context), and any window at least as long as the draft block makes batched verification block-independent by construction. Nine pre-registered GPU batches back these results. Simple models of acceptance, decoding cost and memory, two of them checked on held-out measurements, account for the measured self-speculative speed-ups ($2.09\times$ with the full cache, $2.58\times$ with the deepest plane) and decompose the $2.24\times$ fixed-memory throughput gain of one shared plane.

These conclusions are supported by a complementary cluster mean-field theory which correctly preserves the symmetry of the higher plateaus but leads to the same spontaneous symmetry breaking for the $1/9$ plateau with a qualitatively similar pattern of nine different local magnetizations.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:

The circuit uses only $X$, CNOT, and Toffoli gates under all-to-all connectivity and is classically reversible. Our construction accelerates the controlled ladder underlying addition. We then coordinate inter-block propagation via two short-path forest operations to cut the per-block workspace requirement, yielding a nonrecursive implementation with $O(n)$ gates. Both the gate count and circuit depth are asymptotically optimal.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
We consider the focusing energy supercritical nonlinear Schrödinger equation \begin{equation*} i\partial_tψ+Δψ+|ψ|^{2p}ψ=0 \end{equation*} in dimensions $d\geq11$, with $p\in\mathbb N^\ast$, under the Joseph--Lundgren condition $2p+1>p_{JL}(d)$. For every $ν>ν_0(d,p)$, there exists a radial finite-time type II blow-up solution concentrating the ground state $Q$ in the form \begin{equation*} ψ(t,x)=λ^{\frac{1}{p}}(t)Q(λ(t)x)+ζ(t,x),\quad λ(t)=t^{-\frac12-ν}. \end{equation*} All homogeneous Sobolev norms $\|ψ(t)\|_{\dot H^s}$, $1\leq s<s_c$, remain bounded. The radiation converges to a limiting profile \begin{equation*} ζ^*\in \dot H^s(\mathbb R^d), \qquad s_c<s<s_c+2ν|λ_+|, \end{equation*} where $λ_+$ is determined by the leading correction in the asymptotic expansion of $Q$ at infinity. Our proof combines matched asymptotic expansions across three spatial scales with modified energy estimates. The key ingredient is the systematic treatment of the singular nonlinear background and coupled oscillations generated by the slow algebraic tail of $Q$.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Sensory augmentation (SA) can extend how people perceive and engage with public environments through the body, offering opportunities to support shared multimodal experiences between deaf and hearing visitors. Designing such systems requires understanding which combinations of tactile stimuli and body locations users perceive as acceptable. We examined the perceived acceptability of fictitious yet feasible SA configurations in a museum use-case. Using a modified technology acceptance model, we surveyed 307 deaf and hearing participants about tactile stimulus types and body locations. The results showed significant effects of stimulus type and body location on acceptance, but no interactions with hearing status. Participants generally preferred temperature-based stimuli, subtle movement, texture, and tickling over vibration, and distal over proximal body locations. These findings suggest that tactile SA design should be guided primarily by embodied and contextual factors rather than hearing status, informing future systems for shared multimodal experience in public cultural settings.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
The flip tilt illusion is the misperception of the orientation of the alignment between a pair of dots by 90 degrees. It occurs when the dot-pair contains one black dot and one white dot, is typically visible only in the peripheral visual field. It is predicted by the central-peripheral dichotomy (CPD) theory. Along the visual pathway from retina to downstream stages, our brain admits only a tiny fraction of visual input information for recognition due to a processing bottleneck that starts from the output of the primary visual cortex (V1) along the visual pathway. Accordingly, perception downstream from V1 relies on impoverished information, selected largely by gaze shifts to center the selected content at fovea and additionally by the capacity of the bottleneck even in the central visual field, likely making perceptual hypotheses about the visual scene ambiguous or illusory. To overcome, downstream areas send feedback to upstream areas such as V1 to query for additional information, thereby re-assessing the weights of the initial hypotheses. This perceptual algorithm is termed Feedforward-Feedback-Verify-reWeight (FFVW). To save resources, the feedback query is limited largely to the central visual field. The peripheral visual field is thus vulnerable to perceptual ambiguities and illusions. The CPD theory further predicts that impairing the feedback renders the flip tilt illusion visible in the central visual field. This paper reports a confirmation of the prediction. The feedback is disrupted by masking the visual inputs after a short viewing duration t. Furthermore, the FFVW algorithm is studied by a computational model of the perceptual data as a function of t. It reveals that the initial feedforward sweep of visual information explains the flip tilt illusion for t shorter than 20 ms, whereas the feedback mechanism dominates perception for longer t.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Speech and language technologies have expanded access to communication, but the support they provide is often fixed. The same linguistic or visual aid may help one user and hinder another, or become less useful as task demands change. This project proposes a framework for adapting language presentation to individual abilities and ongoing interaction. It separates access to a message from the estimation of user needs and from the selection of support, including sentence segmentation, pictograms, and optional spoken output. Behavioral feedback provides the primary evidence for adaptation; electroencephalography is considered an additional, uncertainty-aware source of information rather than a direct measure of comprehension. We specify a staged evaluation comparing fixed, behavior-adaptive, and neuroadaptive interfaces. The central question is whether neural information improves comprehension and communication efficiency beyond a strong behavioral baseline.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Passive matching networks are critical components in radio-frequency integrated circuits (RFICs), but their design is bottlenecked by expensive finite-difference-based electromagnetic (EM) simulation. We propose an end-to-end neural framework for free-form RFIC passives that predicts both EM response and downstream design performance under varying frequency and circuit contexts, combining a frequency-conditioned neural simulator with a circuit-conditioned neural solver. To improve design performance prediction, the simulator outputs a neural EM response consisting of both the explicit EM response and a complementary response, together with a dependence regularizer that encourages the two responses to capture orthogonal information. To evaluate the proposed framework, we construct a large-scale dataset of free-form passive layouts, synthesized from both expert-designed contours and random paths. Our 21M-parameter model achieves high accuracy across a broad frequency range, circuit contexts and passive matching settings, with $R^2>0.98$ for almost all targets, while providing orders-of-magnitude faster evaluation than traditional EM simulation. Code available at https://github.com/ETH-IDEAS/RFIC-NeuralSim.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Ferroelectric surfaces exhibit polarization-dependent photoreactivity and provide a route to program chemical patterns through local electrical control of polarization. Observations accumulated over several decades show reaction products in domain interiors, at domain boundaries, and in other selected regions, indicating that the mechanisms extend beyond a single polarization-induced band-bending picture. Here we analyze light-induced charging and interfacial reactions on uniformly polarized ferroelectrics and domain patterns, for dry surfaces and surfaces in contact with an electrochemically active solution. A common semiconductor transport and charge-conservation framework distinguishes five cases: an isolated dry ferroelectric, a dry ferroelectric connected to a carrier reservoir, a blocking ferroelectric-electrolyte junction, a reactive interface with an external carrier return, and two opposite domains coupled through the solid and electrolyte. Analytical solutions and numerical evaluations connect stationary potentials versus illumination to differential optical spectra and finite light-step responses. We further examine the doping effects on static potentials in all five cases and dynamic photovoltage in the isolated film and a fixed-polarization, bare-surface contacted-film variant. For reactive interfaces, the same framework determines reduction and oxidation rates, their spatial distributions, and accumulated reaction amount. The analysis covers surface charging and photochemical conversion beyond deposition, while retaining the electrical and chemical boundaries that distinguish finite charging from sustained turnover, and explains the observed range of photodeposition morphologies. Finally, this framework builds the theoretical foundation for the modulated photovoltage imaging methods that can readily be realized in SPM under illumination.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Achieving safety in autonomous driving through Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is a critical yet challenging task due to non-stationarity, partial observability, and the need for effective coordination among agents. Although earlier cooperative MARL methods have aimed to improve coordination by sharing encoded state observations, we find these strategies are insufficient in safety-critical scenarios. To address this gap, we present IntNet, a novel MARL framework that enhances safety by incorporating the transmission of vehicle intent and adaptive communication scheduling into a unified end-to-end learning paradigm, jointly optimising all components for safe coordination. Central to our approach is an observation prediction module that enables agents to forecast subsequent policy outputs, which they can then share across a vehicle-to-vehicle network. Our model-free architecture employs a Graph Attention Network to process incoming messages and a scheduler component to dynamically optimise the communication graph for bandwidth efficiency. We compare IntNet against state-of-the-art communicative MARL methods in complex urban environments with both autonomous and human-operated vehicles, achieving improved coordination, lower collision rates, and reducing communication efforts by up to 60\%. Through extensive experiments, we assess the framework's learning efficiency, scalability, and the balance between information sharing and bandwidth usage for collision-free trajectories.

Following the evolution of the model through the interaction- and density-driven Mott transitions at zero temperature, we highlight how the three symmetry-resolved components of the two-site entanglement probe different key aspects of Mott and pseudogap physics.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Stacked intelligent metasurfaces (SIMs) cascade programmable layers in front of a feed. In the SIM designs reported so far, including those proposed for low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellites, the layer coefficients are space-only controls or are varied randomly in time to support opportunistic scheduling, so that every radiated beam carries the frequency of the feed. This paper introduces space-time SIMs (ST-SIMs), whose layers are modulated in time and use the temporal dimension of the stack deterministically: each spatial mode of the aperture is paired with its own prescribed frequency translation. The application is LEO broadcasting, where a common waveform reaches terminals with different Doppler shifts, and any common Doppler correction leaves residuals of up to half the Doppler span. We derive the harmonic-domain model of the stack, solve the minimum-energy space-frequency synthesis in closed form, and prove that full column rank of the steering matrix is necessary and sufficient for decoupling K terminal-specific translations, a result that extends to groups of terminals. We further propose a phase-only synthesis algorithm with guaranteed stationarity, together with quantization and control-rate laws. Simulations at 20 GHz over 50 random drops show that a four-layer ST-SIM with a single radio-frequency chain removes the Doppler floor of a static SIM for footprint radii above about 45 km and, under the ideal phase-only model and at equal radiated peak energy, approaches ideal digital per-terminal precompensation within 0.5 dB for resolvable terminals, whereas, in the evaluated geometries, a single time-modulated layer cannot synthesize the required modes.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Path integral control is a stochastic optimal control framework that computes optimal policies as weighted averages over state trajectories. It was recently shown that, combined with stochastic quantum trajectories, the path integral control approach constitutes a promising alternative for quantum optimal control. The change of measure is defined on the driving noise space under an exact control-noise matching condition, which also accommodates rank-deficient state diffusions. Applied to stochastic Schrödinger equations, the resulting formalism gives a compact treatment of paired non-Hermitian jump channels with unequal positive dissipation rates and yields cross-entropy-optimal feedback and open-loop control formulas.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Materials improvements in transmon qubits have yielded remarkable advances in qubit lifetimes (T1)and coherence times (T2). However, state-of-the-art superconducting qubits experience temporal fluctuations in their performance, which limit gate fidelities and quantum processor performance. We observe correlated increases in qubit relaxation and dephasing rates that last for minutes to hours, which we call T1 and T2 excursions. Using interleaved lifetime and coherence time measurements, noise spectroscopy, and two-level-system (TLS) spectroscopy, we find that these excursions are caused by single or few strongly-coupled TLS defects that spectrally diffuse into resonance with the qubit frequency. Our measurement protocol provides a powerful tool for understanding the noise sources that cause temporal fluctuations in superconducting qubit performance.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Distributed quantum protocols require measurement outcomes produced at one node to control operations at another. We present QQLink, a programming and orchestration layer that expresses these dependencies in a single program, using workflow nodes, deferred measurement references, and declared entanglement, and derives the cross-node coordination automatically. Its planner constructs a provably acyclic dependency graph in time linear in the total size of the instructions' qubit footprints. The same programs execute through simulator backends or are lowered to dynamic circuits on partitioned quantum hardware. We evaluate seven protocol workflows. Exhaustive feedforward-branch tests on the simulator runtime path, over tomographically complete input sets, yield output-state infidelities of at most $5\times10^{-12}$ and no incorrect classical outputs, and replaying every plan in random topological orders leaves each final state unchanged. Separate executor processes run the plans with delayed messages, with the joint quantum state held by a centralized simulation service. Every run with the full plan is correct, and removing required cross-node dependencies causes protocol failures. The lowered circuits match hand-written implementations of the same construction in two-qubit gate and conditional-block counts. Runs on two IBM Heron processors, each partitioned into virtual QPUs, demonstrate same-chip execution in two sessions a week apart. The runs also show large variation between sessions and losses beyond what calibration-derived noise models predict. Coherence-sensitive checks do not establish coherent Toffoli operation or preservation of the intended repetition-code superposition. These results support QQLink's workflow semantics on the tested execution paths and identify limits of the current hardware realization; execution across physically networked QPUs remains future work.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
A property-based test (PBT) checks a property of a program on many generated inputs, but writing one takes a property, a generator of valid inputs, and an oracle. LLM-based PBT writers produce all three, yet they have been evaluated only on Python libraries. We study how two of them, Proptest-AI and Agentic-PBT, generalize to ten programs in five domains: deep learning libraries, databases, system software, compilers, and LLM serving engines. Most of these programs take text in their own language, such as queries, configurations, and programs. Agentic-PBT covers more branches than Proptest-AI on seven of the ten programs with Opus 5 and on all ten with GLM-5.3-Flash. Domain-specific fuzzers cover more of the compilers and of PostgreSQL and less of PyTorch than Agentic-PBT. We filed 180 bug reports, 44 of which duplicate reports that others filed after the models' knowledge cutoffs; maintainers have confirmed 65 of the others, in all five domains, and fixed 23. We draw lessons for building and evaluating such writers: low observability hurts them, and mature fuzzers paired with LLM-written properties could check that each feature behaves as documented.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
The data-to-solution map of the incompressible Euler equations is continuous but not uniformly continuous on Sobolev spaces, whereas viscosity makes the Navier--Stokes solution map Lipschitz continuous on small data, uniformly in time. This paper identifies the behavior of the solution map for a hybrid system sitting between these two extremes: the incompressible Oldroyd--B model in $\mathbb{R}^d$, $d=2,3$, in the high-Reynolds-number, high-Weissenberg-number regime. The velocity equation is a forced Euler equation and the only dissipation is a fractional diffusion $η(-Δ)^β$, $\frac12\leβ\le1$, acting on stress. We prove that, on the ball of small $H^s$ data ($s>1+\frac d2$) on which global solutions exist, the solution map is Lipschitz continuous with respect to the $H^{r}$-norm, $r=s-(2β-1)$, uniformly for all time, and Lipschitz into the natural dissipation spaces; the constant is explicit and tends to $\sqrt3$ as the size of the data tends to zero. Consequently the map is Hölder continuous into $C_b([0,\infty);H^{s'})$ for every $s'<s$, and is Lipschitz in $H^s$ itself when $β=\frac12$. Thus, although the velocity field is only transported, the solution map behaves like that of the Navier--Stokes equations rather than that of the Euler equations. The proof exploits the damped wave structure generated by the coupling between $u$ and $\nabla\cdotτ$ through a Lyapunov functional with a cross term $(δu,\nabla\cdotδτ)_{H^{r-β}}$, which transfers the stress dissipation to the velocity difference, together with a low-frequency interpolation argument that keeps all Gronwall coefficients integrable on $(0,\infty)$. The loss of $2β-1$ derivatives is exactly the gap between the hidden velocity dissipation of order $2(1-β)$ and the dissipation required by the Lipschitz estimate, and we show that it cannot be reduced by the energy method.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Requirements traceability links support activities such as change-impact analysis, coverage checking, and validation. Industrial requirements can include traceable images, which text-only approaches cannot process directly. For a fixed classifier configuration, binary decisions alone offer no direct way to adjust the balance between missed and incorrect links. We extend a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach for inter-requirements traceability link recovery (TLR). Our extension retrieves text and image candidates separately, classifies each retrieved pair with a vision-language model, and filters the predicted links by verbalized confidence. We evaluate our approach on three non-overlapping industrial requirement sets and six public text-only datasets. On the industrial test sets, our approach achieves an F1 score of 0.310, compared with 0.114 for our replication of the baseline approach by Hey et al. Our approach recovers links in all four modality combinations while improving text-only F1 on the industrial data and maintaining similar performance on the public datasets, but recovery remains limited by failures to retrieve related text requirements for image queries. Confidence filtering produces link sets with different precision and recall, removing false positives and some correctly recovered links from the unfiltered link set. This study provides industrial evidence on the potential and limitations of a current RAG-based TLR approach for multimodal requirements and identifies cross-modal retrieval as the component to prioritize in further optimization.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Amorphous solid-state electrolytes (SSEs) are attractive candidates for safe, high-energy-density all-solid-state batteries. The recent discovery that amorphous LiTaCl$_6$ and LiNbCl$_6$ reach room-temperature ionic conductivities above 10 mS cm$^{-1}$ with activation energies below 0.2 eV has spurred a broad search for new amorphous halide Li conductors. Here we report a computational screening of amorphous lithium trivalent-metal chlorides (Li-M(III)-Cl) using molecular dynamics driven by a universal machine-learning force field. For the sixteen Li-M(III)-Cl compositions spanning fifteen rare-earth elements and indium, all phases exhibit fast room-temperature Li$^+$ diffusion, with diffusivities of roughly $2$-$5 \times 10^{-7}$ cm$^2$ s$^{-1}$. After scaling the conductivity versus diffusivity relation to an experimental LiTaCl$_6$ reference, the estimated room-temperature conductivities range from 7.7 mS cm$^{-1}$ for amorphous Li$_3$InCl$_6$ to 14 mS cm$^{-1}$ for amorphous Li$_3$ScCl$_6$. With a low activation energy of 0.18 eV, amorphous Li$_3$ScCl$_6$ is predicted to be among the most conductive amorphous halide electrolytes. Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Using vector magnetogram data from the Helioseismic Magnetic Imager (HMI) on board the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO), we present detailed case studies of precursor activity in Active Regions (ARs) 13664 and 13842, which produced several intense flares. We examined the spatiotemporal evolution of key magnetic topological parameters, including winding, helicity, winding-flux-based masked polarity inversion lines (PILs), and PIL gradients, from the precursor to the post-flare phases. The temporal evolution of the winding flux showed a significant enhancement during the precursor phase, and this trend was consistent across the seven X-class and five M-class flares (>= M5.0). The spatial distribution of both raw and Gaussian-smoothed winding-flux enhancement is co-located with flare footpoint regions of highly twisted core fields, as indicated by the photospheric magnetic topology. The winding-flux-based masked PILs that persisted around the flare locations showed a significant increase in strength and area during the precursor activity. These masked PILs spatially coincide with regions likely hosting non-potential core magnetic fields associated with the observed flares. Furthermore, the gradient of strong PILs extracted from the ARs was positively correlated with flare-associated locations and typically increased several hours (approx. 3-5 h) before flare onset. By imposing a gradient threshold on strong PILs, we isolate magnetic regions repeatedly associated with flare initiation, providing useful constraints in regimes where current flare-forecasting models remain uncertain. Therefore, the combined analysis of the spatiotemporal evolution of different magnetic topological parameters enhances our understanding of intense solar flare forecasting and the identification of potential triggering sites, thereby contributing to improved space weather prediction frameworks.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Models transporting overall survival (OS) effects across clinical trials fail when they ignore the "post-progression treatment regime"---the subsequent therapy rates across biomarker strata and randomized arms. Because this trial-level regime is systematically omitted from published reports, standard correction families are structurally inadequate: crossover adjustments target an unrealistic counterfactual with zero subsequent therapy, erasing critical environmental differences; population adjustments (including MAIC, STC, AIPW, and density ratios) match baseline individual covariates, leaving trial-level regimes mismatched. We show that these correction approaches carry near-identical bias, proving the failure is informational rather than methodological. Simulations demonstrate that ignoring the target setting's landscape can leave the directional sign of the transported effect completely undetermined, even when mechanisms are fully known. Conversely, providing the target regime to a regime-aware estimator successfully recovers the true treatment effect. Code is available at https://github.com/felizzi/post-progression-transport-WMHS-NeurIPS-2026.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Magnetic switchbacks are mostly Alfvénic local deflections, or even reversals, of the ambient magnetic field of the solar wind. Despite intense research their origin remains unclear and is highly debated. Here we describe a new simulation study demonstrating how torsional Alfvén waves can evolve into switchbacks. We use surface rotational motions to launch torsional Alfvén waves into the super-radially expanding magnetic field of a coronal hole. The simulations demonstrate that in such an expanding wind, the waves initially steepen as they propagate while also inducing a cylindrical parallel plasma jet. A combination of shear from the jet and wave evolution under the constraint of approximate spherical polarisation ($|\mathbf{B}|\approx const.$) then leads to the formation of switchbacks in a ring configuration. We explore the 3D nature of the switchbacks, how and where they from, and present scalings for their peak deflection and parallel and perpendicular length scales. We also derive an expression for switchback deflection in the linear regime which we contrast against our results. The results are discussed in relation to recent observations and previous switchback formation studies.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Actor frameworks on mainstream runtimes advertise Erlang/OTP-style supervision, but OTP's consistency contracts assume a synchronous, single-threaded supervisor, and ports inherit that assumption's absence as unexamined risk. We evaluated every supervision guarantee against pinned OTP documentation and source read verbatim, against the source of three further Rust actor frameworks at fixed revisions, and against the actor-model literature, recording the evidence behind each design decision. Blind adversarial audits and the cross-framework study surfaced 24 defect classes, of which eight reduce to one root cause: reconstructing, by explicit mechanism, the atomicity a synchronous supervisor gets implicitly. We introduce a supervision runtime that closes all 24 cataloged classes through supervisor-owned completion values, per-incarnation identity, and a single lifecycle state machine, validated by 241 tests including reverted-fix reproductions. The result holds OTP's verbatim-verified contracts while adding two properties OTP does not offer: a supervisor that remains responsive throughout group restarts, and message handlers that are never cancelled mid-execution. We delimit the forcing guarantees no cooperative runtime can honor.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:

We study the spectrum of $L$ using the perturbative determinant which is known to determine its spectrum and to admit a product representation similar to that of the generating function in KdV. We use this to show that the dynamics of the integrals of motion constructed in \cite{BoitiManfrin2026,BHMP,campos} admits a Lax pair formulation with the same operator $L$ and to get a new proof of the involutivity of these integrals.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Identifying prodromal Parkinson's Disease is a precondition for any future treatment that modifies the course of the disease, since such therapies would ideally act on the initial pathogenic events, early enough to delay the clinical onset of the disease rather than only slow its progression. In this work, a visual exploration model is retrained on an expanded corpus. Without any further training or threshold recalibration, it is then tested on an enriched cohort of patients with high risk of being in the prodromal phase of Parkinson's Disease, testing whether the learned signal follows a continuum of disease rather than only separating patients from controls. The resulting score distribution is analysed as an external evaluation of the hypothesis that the oculomotor signature targeted by the model is already partly present before clinical diagnosis. With every subject scored on data not used to train the model, the scores are ordered as controls < high-risk patients < Parkinson's Disease, with 42% of the high-risk patients exceeding the decision threshold. A SHAP decomposition of the scores into classifiers and gaze features shows that high scores in this cohort are driven mainly by reduced saccadic excursion, fewer fixations and longer fixations, the hypokinetic oculomotor profile that characterises Parkinson's Disease. The model score is also compared against the prodromal markers used for recruitment. The score is not correlated with hyposmia, constipation, depression or REM sleep behaviour disorder; these results, interpreted in the context of the selection induced by the recruitment criteria, are discussed as evidence that within the high-risk cohort the score is largely not explained by the available ancillary clinical variables. The results suggest that the visual biomarkers analysed are a complementary indicator to identify patients at risk of being in the prodromal stage.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
A prime gap $(p_n, p_{n+1})$ is \textit{frangible} if the smallest prime divisor of every integer $m$ with $p_n<m<p_{n+1}$ is strictly less than the size of the gap, $p_{n+1}-p_n$. Gafni and Tao recently proved that the number of frangible gaps up to $X$ is $\ll X/\log^2 X$, answering a question of Erdős. They also showed that under the Dickson--Hardy--Littlewood prime tuples conjecture this number is $\sim c X/\log^2 X$ for a constant $c$, for which they obtained a rough estimate. We describe improved methods for estimating this constant under the same hypothesis, and establish that its value lies in $[2.7416, 2.7984]$, confirming a speculation of Gafni and Tao. In addition, we present the results of a complete survey of frangible gaps up to $10^{17}$. An ensuing empirical measurement of $c$ matches our estimate very well.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Geometric tailoring of magnetic responses is a central theme in modern magnetism. By employing cross-sectional geometric modulation, we investigate how geometric variations influence the dynamics of field-driven domain walls. This approach enables the realization of a domain-wall trap, achieved through a nanostripe constriction, and a domain-wall diode, realized via a wedge-shaped expansion. We demonstrate that domain walls can be efficiently pinned by cross-sectional modulation, with the depinning field exhibiting strong dependence on the cross-sectional gradient. Under weak applied fields, the domain wall undergoes localized oscillations near the pinning site; under strong fields, this pinning breaks down, reproducing the typical diode characteristics. Theoretical calculations based on a biaxial ferromagnet model and a collective-variable approach are in excellent agreement with micromagnetic simulations. Finally, we delineate the parameter regime for realistic samples in which these predicted effects are most pronounced.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly wired to consequential tools that send public alerts, dispatch responders, and query citizen records, where one erroneous tool call carries real-world cost. Existing agent-safety benchmarks measure generic harm or prompt-injection success and implicitly treat refusing as the safe default. In public-safety deployments that assumption breaks: an agent too cautious to dispatch help fails as surely as one that triggers a false alert. We present SentryBench, which scores agents on a two-sided, cost-sensitive frontier jointly measuring attack success, over-refusal (missing a real emergency), and over-reaction (unwarranted action) under adversarial tool use, with scenarios grounded in real emergency-call transcripts, disaster messages, and real injection/jailbreak payloads. We formalize deployment harm as an asymmetric cost functional, prove naive caution is harm-dominated whenever it refuses more genuine emergencies than the attack harm it averts, and prove a targeted trust gate adds zero over-refusal on clean input. Across 840 scored episodes over three frontier models and three defenses, refuse-more caution drives over-refusal to 100 percent on two of three models for at most a 3.7-point change in attack success and yields the worst harm everywhere, whereas our trust-gating wrapper dominates the frontier (lowest harm on every model, over-refusal at or below baseline, higher containment). Provider content filters also silently perform part of the defending and must be reported separately.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:

At zero field, the spectrum exhibits the canonical multi-spinon continuum of the Heisenberg chain. With increasing field we demonstrate the appearance of an energy gap $2Δ$ towards momentum $q\rightarrow 0$ between the uniform magnetization precession mode and the shifted spinon continuum. $2Δ$ is a direct measure of spinon backscattering interactions. Comparison with numerical matrix-product-state calculations and a recent analytical theory shows excellent agreement. By examining the integrable spin-1/2 chain, we provide an example of how quasiparticle interactions can be quantified experimentally in isotropic quantum spin systems.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:

We propose Dual Gradient Consensus (DGC), an adaptive-learning method for mixed in-domain/out-domain disturbances that retains the random Fourier feature model, offline BPTT policy, and least-squares adaptation of a prior domain-adaptive residual policy (DAPL) while modifying the online update step size. DGC compares each residual gradient with long- and short-term gradient memories, classifies the current adaptation regime, and uses a confidence map to suppress unreliable updates while recovering adaptation after persistent domain shifts. We evaluate DGC in numerical quadrotor trajectory tracking under four residuals that mix an in-domain component with short out-domain events. Compared with $L_1$-augmented MPC, RFF-based MPC, constant-step DAPL, and a frozen-parameter baseline, DGC achieves the lowest mean position RMSE in all four cases.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Autonomous agents have been observed acting beyond their assigned tasks, accessing unauthorized systems, and establishing communication channels to exchange information, yet the Web and network-level techniques they use to extend their capabilities and circumvent security restrictions remain poorly understood. We study these techniques through the ProWiki incident, in which agents restricted to outbound HTTP GET requests repurposed a public German-language wiki as a message board. We analyze 14,591 agent edits containing 79,541 URL postings and present corroborating evidence that the published URLs reflect the agents' operational activity. We find that 26,717 URL occurrences (33.6%) embed target URLs within one to five layers of third-party Web services. By recursively reconstructing these nested URLs, we identify 67 distinct intermediate services and classify their functionality. Most intermediate layers (73.8%) extend agents' capabilities by delegating content extraction and transformation to external Web services: Markdown and OCR services convert web content into machine-readable text, JSON filtering services extract selected fields, and archival services expose historical versions of pages. The remaining 26.2% facilitate circumvention of access restrictions and evasion of detection, including CORS and fetch proxies that retrieve content on agents' behalf, and link shorteners and redirectors that hide destination URLs from mechanisms inspecting literal URLs or outer hostnames. Agents also reach the same targets through multiple URL paths, consistent with attempts to evade rate limits or obscure request origins. Our results expose a gap between the capabilities granted to agents and those they can obtain by composing publicly available Web services: restricting an agent's local toolset or direct Internet access may be insufficient while third-party services remain reachable.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Kernel techniques are among the most powerful methods in data science and statistics. One of the key properties of kernels contributing to their numerous successful applications is that the associated reproducing kernel Hilbert space is expressive enough to encode probability distributions without loss of information or to capture the joint independence of $M\ge 2$ random variables, under mild conditions. Computationally, these measures (i) rely on the so-called Gram matrix which contains the pairwise similarity of sample points, and (ii) converge at a rate $O \left(n^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)$, where $n$ denotes the sample size. We focus on measuring the independence of latent position random graphs (LPRGs), a model widely-applied for instance in neuroscience, sociology, and epidemiology. In LPRGs a latent representation is associated to each node. The similarity of these representations (meant via a kernel) determines whether two nodes are connected, making the Gram matrices only implicitly observable and the estimation challenging. Despite the fundamental importance of quantifying the independence of $M$ LPRGs, very little is known about the solution of this problem; existing techniques are restricted to $M=2$ components and only guarantee consistency without rates. In this work, (i) we define an independence measure called graph Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion (GHSIC) for $M\ge 2$ LPRGs, (ii) we prove that it can be estimated at a rate $\tilde{O}\left(n^{-\frac{1}{3}}\right)$ relying on spectral decomposition of adjacency matrices, (iii) without the need to choose kernels and their hyperparameters. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed GHSIC estimator both on synthetic examples and in the analysis of brain functional connectivity subnetworks in natural language perception.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Foundation models provide powerful representations for unstructured data, such as text and images, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) makes their adaptation to downstream tasks increasingly practical. For neural estimators that lack a tractable sampling distribution, resampling-based procedures offer a flexible route to statistical inference, but they often require hundreds of model fits, making them computationally prohibitive at foundation-model scale. We introduce HIFI, a two-stage fine-tuning framework for statistical inference on parameters such as conditional means. Stage 1 adapts a foundation model once on a larger sample, capturing the complex structure of the data and controlling estimation bias through a single fit. Stage 2 applies a resampling inference procedure to a smaller independent sample, concurrently fitting multiple lightweight PEFT estimators to the residual to quantify estimation variability without relearning the full task. HIFI accommodates a broad class of resampling procedures, including ensemble subsampling and the nonparametric bootstrap. Across vision and text experiments, HIFI scales to pretrained models ranging from tens of millions to more than ten billion parameters while providing accurate point estimates and well-calibrated confidence intervals across diverse architectures, and reduces training compute by up to 91.9% relative to direct resampling. An application to gene-expression inference illustrates the practical value of the framework for uncertainty-aware scientific inference.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
JWST has uncovered a population of compact high-redshift galaxies, 'little red dots' (LRDs), exhibiting broad Balmer emission lines that often show narrow absorption features and strong Balmer breaks - spectral signatures attributed to dense gas surrounding rapidly growing black holes, but whose small-scale structure remains unknown. A striking feature of LRD spectra is that the H$β$ absorption is systematically deeper than H$α$, yet in any homogeneous gas this ordering is physically impossible. Here we model the H$α$ and H$β$ line profiles using radiative transfer simulations for 11 LRDs with JWST sensitive high resolution spectroscopy, and independently constrain the $n=2$ hydrogen column density, $N_{\rm HI,\mathit{n}=2}$, from the Balmer-break continuum. We find that the $N_{\rm HI,\mathit{n}=2}$ from H$α$ in a homogeneous medium cannot reproduce the observed H$β$ absorption in several objects, and that this $N_{\rm HI,\mathit{n}=2}$ typically falls two orders of magnitude below the lower bound set by the Balmer break. Both tensions are simultaneously resolved by a multiphase medium of dense clumps within diffuse hot ionized gas. This multiphase gas structure is a necessary ingredient for any viable LRD model, regardless of the nature of the central engine.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Let $\mathcal O_K$ be the ring of integers of a number field $K$. A finite subset $\mathcal H=\{η_1,\ldots,η_k\}\subset\mathcal O_K$ is said to be \emph{admissible} if for every prime ideal $\mathfrak p$ in $\mathcal O_K$, the reductions of the $η_i$ modulo $\mathfrak p$ do not represent every residue class. The diameter of a finite subset $S$ of $\mathcal O_K$ is defined to be \[\mathrm{diam}(S):= \max_{η_i,η_j\in S:η_i\neqη_j}|\mathcal N(η_i-η_j)|\] where $\mathcal N$ denotes the norm down to the rational field. This paper computationally investigates admissible subsets of rings of integers in imaginary quadratic fields of class number 1 (such as the Gaussian integers or the Eisenstein integers) that are large relative to their diameter. The motivation is twofold. Firstly, there is the improvement of results analogous to the question of an upper bound for the least gap between large rational primes, which has been one of the great number theoretic successes of the twenty-first century. A second motivation is that there is the opportunity to disprove a variation of the second Hardy-Littlewood conjecture. The calculations in the paper provide new records on the smallest distance between primes in the fields in question, and explicit counter-examples to a generalisation of the second Hardy-Littlewood conjecture in all bar one of the fields.
