Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
As superconducting quantum processors scale to large qubit counts, unwanted microwave drive crosstalk becomes an important source of coherent errors. Here, we investigate the role of parasitic coupling paths in the suppression of drive crosstalk in a processor with two fixed-frequency transmon qubits and a tunable coupler. To account for the many different coupling paths, we develop a detailed circuit model to capture the dependence of crosstalk on the coupler frequency. We experimentally demonstrate suppression of crosstalk, finding that the suppression does not originate solely from cancellation of the effective qubit-qubit coupling, but also is a result of interference between other coupling paths. Building on these insights, we show that drive crosstalk can be suppressed with the right choice of parasitic capacitances, which otherwise often are treated as unwanted design imperfections. Our results provide practical guidance for low-crosstalk device design of superconducting quantum processors and point toward a broader strategy in which parasitic coupling paths are engineered rather than simply minimized.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
We tackle the challenge of building real-time interactive video worlds with user-defined behaviors. Such worlds must track object states, apply interaction rules, and render the resulting consequences as users act. Yet existing end-to-end video world models typically learn interaction dynamics within the generator, making it difficult to specify object-level rules and reason about their consequences. In this work, we introduce BoxWorld, which separates interaction reasoning from generative rendering. Given user-specified rules, a coding agent creates a Box World Engine that determines interaction outcomes and exposes the resulting object states through a lightweight interface of layout boxes, persistent object attributes, and dynamic status variables, leaving appearance and physical effects to generative rendering. A Box-State Generative Renderer then renders this evolving state stream into video autoregressively, enabling online control over object motion, state switches, and conditional events. Rendering this state stream is non-trivial: the renderer must respond to object-level state updates in real time while remaining coherent with the generated history. To this end, we introduce a three-stage training strategy that learns object grounding from open-domain videos and state transitions from gameplay videos, both annotated automatically, and finally performs rollout distillation on self-generated histories. We further propose PairedStateBench, a paired benchmark for fine-grained interaction control. BoxWorld substantially outperforms end-to-end world models and remains competitive across multiple public benchmarks. Project page: https://boxworld-web.github.io.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Robotic agents operating in real-world environments must adapt continuously from a stream of multimodal demonstrations, often under constraints that preclude storing or revisiting past data. In this replay-free, single-pass lifelong imitation learning setting, sequential updates can progressively distort the representation space, making expert-based approaches particularly sensitive to routing interference, causing expert selection to degrade over time. We propose HIDRA, a structured routing framework that mitigates this issue through a hierarchical dual-attention mechanism, which decouples instruction-level expert retrieval from context-dependent refinement. To further stabilize routing under representation drift, HIDRA introduces a key-level geometric regularization that enforces both alignment within tasks and separation across tasks. The resulting approach enables reliable expert selection while supporting an expandable set of experts for continual adaptation. We evaluate HIDRA on several LIBERO benchmark suites, including more challenging variants with heterogeneous task sequences and paraphrased language instructions. Our approach consistently outperforms both replay-free and replay-based baselines, improving AUC and forward transfer while maintaining low forgetting, with stronger gains under high interference and language variation. The code is available at: https://github.com/yfqi/HIDRA.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Artificial intelligence (AI) shows promise for breast imaging, but limited labeled data, institutional data fragmentation, and privacy concerns hinder centralized training. We investigate a privacy-aware federated learning framework combining pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) with client-level differential privacy. We compare general-purpose CLIP models, biomedical BiomedCLIP, and an ImageNet-pretrained ViT-B/16 baseline on two public breast imaging datasets, with and without differential privacy. We also evaluate a CLIP ViT-B/16 ablation that removes the text pathway. Evaluation includes patient-level ROC-AUC with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, baseline comparisons, threshold sensitivity, inter-model agreement, and communication cost. Under federated learning, all five models achieve high normal-versus-sick discrimination (ROC-AUC: 0.940-0.990). However, acquisition year alone achieves 0.974 on the same test partition, raising concerns about confounding rather than genuine pathology recognition. Benign-versus-malignant discrimination remains uncertain (ROC-AUC: 0.504-0.637), with all confidence intervals including 0.50. Removing the text pathway preserves classification accuracy while halving communication cost. Differential privacy reduces ROC-AUC by 0.375, attributable to perturbing the full model state rather than only trainable parameters. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating confounding, predictive reliability, privacy implementation, and deployment efficiency when developing federated AI systems for breast imaging.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Let $c>1$ be irrational. We prove that, for almost every $x>0$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there are infinitely many triples $(p,r,s)$, with $p$ and $r$ prime and $s$ an integer, for which \[ 0<px-r<p^{-1/3+\varepsilon},\qquad 0<pcx-s<p^{-1/3+\varepsilon}. \] This improves the exponent $1/5$ in the homogeneous-line case of a theorem of Baier and Ghosh. The arithmetic input is the quantitative prime-counting lower bound in Matomäki's proof concerning primes in shrinking neighborhoods of an irrational rotation. We obtain a local first-moment lower bound by fixing the prime numerator and applying the prime number theorem to the admissible prime denominators. Two Selberg sieve squares, together with explicit trigonometric interval approximations, give a pointwise upper bound whose error tends to zero in $L^1$ after normalization. A truncation and density-point argument then yields the almost-everywhere conclusion.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
In this paper we study shape optimization problems for planar convex sets with prescribed minimal width or constant width. We prove that the Reuleaux triangle minimizes torsional rigidity among sets of constant width. We also show that the first Dirichlet-Laplace eigenvalue is maximized by the equilateral triangle under a minimal width constraint and by the Reuleaux triangle under a constant width constraint. The proofs use subsets consisting of a disk and three straight or circular caps. Reflection arguments reduce the study to equilateral configurations, which contain a polygon or a disk polygon depending on one parameter. The same cap constructions give a common proof of the known area, Cheeger and inner parallel area inequalities, and yield sharp bounds for all positive moments of the distance to the boundary. We also prove sharp inequalities for concentric disk intersections and decreasing radial integrals, and compare interaction energies for kernels close to a positive constant. This includes a nonempty interval of positive Riesz exponents. Finally, we investigate whether inclusion monotonicity and Minkowski concavity suffice to obtain these comparisons for other functionals.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Cavity quantum magnonics has ushered in an unprecedented era of hybrid light-matter interfaces in which microwave photons, collective spin excitations, and superconducting or spin qubits can be coupled within a single device architecture, facilitating a versatile platform for quantum information processing. Realizing their full potential, however, requires a theory that can treat non-reciprocal magnetic media, material dissipation and open-cavity radiation losses, as well as finite-temperature fluctuations rigorously and without significant approximation. The dissipative magnonic resonances of such systems are described as quasinormal modes (QNMs), yet a consistent quantization procedure for lossy gyrotropic resonators has remained elusive. In this work, we present a finite-temperature quantum QNM theory, based on macroscopic quantum electrodynamics for non-reciprocal media and complex coordinate transformations, that achieves QNM quantization for a wide class of spatially inhomogeneous, dissipative and dispersive, cavity magnonic systems. We demonstrate the predictive capabilities of our theory via applications to hybrid dielectric-magnonic resonators interacting with both spin and superconducting qubits, evidencing modal interference effects, a continuous transition from coherent to dissipative coupling, spatiotemporal quantum field dynamics, and magnon-mediated qubit synchronization, at both zero and finite temperatures. By addressing the intricacies of modal loss and non-reciprocity in a fully quantum theory of cavity magnonics, our approach enables the quantitative design of hybrid quantum devices that operate under realistic open-system and thermal conditions, without recourse to ad hoc quantization schemes.

We report electrical tuning of spin relaxation in atomically thin $T_{\rm d}$-MoTe$_2$, a representative low-symmetry transition metal dichalcogenide. Weak antilocalization measurements reveal strong spin--orbit interaction with spin--orbit lengths of tens of nanometers, consistent with recent theoretical predictions. Despite the semimetallic nature of $T_{\rm d}$-MoTe$_2$, in the ultrathin limit the spin--orbit scattering time can be tuned electrostatically by up to threefold. We further investigate vertical electric field effects on the spin--orbit length and time, and demonstrate the modulation of the Rashba parameters. Relation between spin--orbit scattering time and the diffusion coefficient indicates that spin relaxation is governed by the D'yakonov--Perel' mechanism in both monolayer and bilayer $T_{\rm d}$-MoTe$_2$. These results establish few-layer $T_{\rm d}$-MoTe$_2$ as a platform for electrically tunable spin transport, thereby providing insight into spin relaxation in low-symmetry transition metal dichalcogenides.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
The Kotani-Last problem and the Deift conjecture are two well known statements, which both concern the almost periodicity properties of the functions under consideration, and which have both been disproved in their original formulation, which involves Bohr/Bochner almost periodicity. To contrast these disproofs, and to further elucidate the essence of these two challenging problems, we establish positive results regarding each of them by showing that Weyl almost periodicity can be deduced whenever the Sodin-Yuditskii setup can be implemented. The latter requires that the Schrödinger operator associated with the function in question has purely absolutely continuous spectral measure and a spectrum with finite total gap length and the Parreau-Widom property. We also show that the known examples for which Bohr/Bochner almost periodicity has been shown or suggested to fail in the context of the Deift conjecture are in fact Weyl almost periodic. As a result, an accordingly modified version of the Deift conjecture remains a tantalizing open problem.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
TrackJoint is a Modelica MultiBody component that turns a three-dimensional road surface into a joint with two degrees of freedom. The two joint coordinates are the distance travelled along a reference line and the sideways offset from that line. Together they give the position, orientation and angular velocity of a single frame_b connector. All road geometry reaches the joint as a small set of periodic piecewise-quintic splines, so one component can represent any circuit whose splines have been fitted beforehand. The road constraint is closed with d'Alembert's principle. The two generalized forces that belong to the joint coordinates are set to zero, so no Lagrange multipliers are needed. The joint is connected to a multibody race car in Dymola and the pair is exported as one FMI~3.0 FMU. The same FMU is then used for time-domain simulation and for CasADi/IPOPT minimum lap-time optimization, with no change to the model in between. This works because the joint keeps the arc-length coordinate as a real state and publishes its time derivative, which is the quantity that lets the problem be rewritten with distance We report results for minimum lap time simulations on the Singapore Formula~1 circuit.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Daily item co-occurrence embeddings are paired with next-day behavior without future-behavior leakage. Multi-day click-through rate (CTR) training therefore mixes versions whose directions and norms may differ for the same item. We compare Word2Vec and an item-graph XSimGCL adaptation across initialization, inheritance, post-processing, training constraints, and downstream augmentation. The inventory contains 48 configurations, including 32 common-protocol CTR evaluations. Observed metrics are reported as relative percentage changes from the corresponding Word2Vec baseline (0%), with raw values and exact dataset sizes withheld. Three findings emerge. First, multiple upstream interventions improve compatibility and CTR. ID-init and orthogonal alignment increase cosine by 51.2% and 93.4%, and GAUC by 2.2% and 2.6%, relative to ordinary Word2Vec. Retrieval and geometry remain insufficient downstream surrogates. Second, warm starts perform strongly but accumulate scale. The day-matched norm increase over Word2Vec reaches 102.5% after eight days; daily global rescaling limits it to 8.2% and attains the highest observed GAUC increase, 4.0%. Third, CTR learning through a dimensionality-reducing encoder further adapts to residual drift. Against dimension-matched random-projection, SVD, and untrained-network controls, trained encoders attain the highest cross-day cosine for four of six upstream methods. The other two rank third and second in train-to-test cosine. These industrial results support complementary roles for upstream stabilization, inherited-scale management, and downstream task learning.

An integral form of their known exponential generating function yields mixtures of uniform distributions and convergent double series. We recover Eulerian polynomial identities and give a probabilistic interpretation of anti-diagonal sums of poly-Bernoulli numbers. We also prove moment determinacy, characterize the Stieltjes parameter range, derive Hankel total non-negativity and log-convexity, and identify the boundary distributions.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Compact electroencephalography (EEG) decoders enable embedded brain--computer interfaces (BCIs), but compression can alter adversarial robustness without proportional hardware savings. We present ORBITAL, a robustness-constrained framework combining hardware-realizable structured compression, recovery-aware operating-point selection, multi-attack evaluation, and native edge validation. Across nine subjects and three seeds on BCI Competition IV-2a, S25-TRADES achieves the highest observed mean true-union robustness among compressed EEGNet models (23.06% vs 21.27% for standard Full), with 26.27% fewer parameters and 25.10% fewer MACs. Matched controls identify TRADES as the main source of robustness recovery, improving S25 union accuracy by 6.74 percentage points over clean recovery (p=0.0039), while per-example analysis reveals boundary redistribution rather than uniform margin expansion. On Jetson Orin Nano, FP16 compression reduces board energy by up to 16.20% and latency by 8.00%. Despite 99.3% prediction agreement, native INT8 Q/DQ incurs about twice the FP16 latency and energy, demonstrating the need for joint robustness and hardware-aware optimization.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Generative AI can produce code, tests, documentation, and technical explanations that resemble artefacts traditionally used as evidence of student competence, weakening the inference from artefact quality to the engineering capability behind it. We report the redesign and first deployment of a 13-week, AI-permissive, software-intensive engineering course in which students may delegate substantial work to AI while retaining responsibility for planning, verification, review, integration, and explanation. The redesign couples an engineering accountability workflow, which structures human-AI work and preserves human decision authority, with an assessment evidence architecture comprising six complementary channels: product, process/origin, verification, explanation, reflection, and individual assurance. A collect--cross-check--escalate (CCE) reasoning logic connects these channels rather than treating any single artefact or trace as sufficient evidence of competence. By the end of Week 11, the deployment involved 87 students organised into 17 teams, with 957 individual weekly Git repositories and 34 group-project Git repositories supporting repeated assessment and engineering activity. The first deployment yielded four practical lessons: AI assistance changes where rubric criteria carry evidential weight; multiple evidence channels require deliberate cross-checking and meaningful complementarity; the evidential strength realised in practice may differ from that intended in the assessment design; and automation scales evidence collection more readily than interpretation. The contribution is a conceptually grounded, deployed design for making engineering responsibility and competence more visible when AI can perform substantial artefact production.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
We present Scalable Pixel-anchored End-to-end Diffusion (SpeeDiff), a latent diffusion method that jointly trains the VAE and the diffusion model from scratch. In principle, joint training allows the diffusion loss gradient to directly guide the VAE encoder, encouraging the formation of a generation-friendly latent space and potentially yielding faster convergence than the conventional two-stage approach with a pretrained frozen VAE. However, a naive end-to-end implementation severely degrades performance, as unrestricted backpropagation of the diffusion loss leads to latent space collapse. Our main technical contribution is a simple yet effective Tweedie Pixel Reconstruction (TPR) loss, which provides additional pixel-level feedback by decoding a predicted clean latent from an intermediate noisy state using Tweedie's formula, thereby alleviating collapse. Furthermore, our method enables jointly scaling a fully transformer-based architecture and enhances representation alignment within the end-to-end framework. Our SpeeDiff-XL model achieves over 140x and 61x faster training compared to Vanilla SiT and REPA, respectively, while attaining an FID of 1.50 without guidance on ImageNet 256x256 generation. With a more efficient 32x compressed VAE, our model further reaches an FID of 1.53 without guidance on ImageNet 512x512 generation.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Two new Bohr-Sommerfeld (B-S) type quantization conditions for $d$-dimensional radial potentials are proposed for non-singular and singular potentials, respectively. The power-like potentials \hbox{$V=\operatorname{sign}(m)\,r^m$} for $m=-3/2,-1,-1/2, 1,3,4,6$ and $V=\log r$ (that corresponds to $m=0$) are studied in detail for radial quantum numbers $n_r \in [0,100]$ and for angular momenta $\ell=1,2,3,4,5$ in dimensions $d=2,3$. It is shown that for large $n_r$ the B-S energies $E_{BS}$ always tend to the exact ones. For $m=2$ (the radial harmonic oscillator) and $m=-1$ (the $d$-dimensional analogue of the $3D$ Coulomb potential) the B-S spectrum coincides with the exact one for the first and second quantization conditions, respectively. In general, up to a small parametric shift of the radial quantum number, the analytic formulas for the energy spectrum can be written for arbitrary power-like potential. A comparison of $E_{BS}$ with the energies $E^{(L)}_{BS}$, obtained for the radial potentials modified by the Langer correction for $d=3$, are in good agreement in general: in detail, it was checked for the quartic oscillator $V=r^4$. It is demonstrated that introducing a dimensionless {\it WKB correction} $γ$ into the r.h.s. of the proposed B-S type quantization condition allows us to reproduce the exact energies with $γ$ being very small for positive degrees $m \geq 0$ and sufficiently small for non-positive ones $m < 0$ for all $n_r, \ell$ studied.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Attack logs and red-team reports show targets the attacks used against them, to help them repair their defenses. Prompt injections against large language models (LLMs) are plain text, so such records also hand targets a working copy. Drawing on social learning theory and work on the victim-offender overlap, we study what targets do with that copy in Tensor Trust, an online game whose players defended LLM-guarded accounts, attacked one another's, and could read every attack they received. Using all 563,349 attack records, we compare each received attack with matched attacks that circulated among similar players at the same moment but never reached the target. Reuse mainly followed success: within a week, targets attacked other players with 10.0% of the attacks that had broken their defense, versus 0.03% of matched attacks (adjusted difference: 8.8-10.0 percentage points). Near-misses, whose replies began with "access granted" but that scored as failures, were reused about as rarely as failures: reuse tracked whether an attack paid off, not how its reply read, consistent with payoff-biased social learning. Breaches were also followed by defense changes, after which same-family attacks became 24.5 percentage points less successful against the target, relative to other defenders. Reuse came mainly from players already attacking, not newcomers. Previously received texts accounted for 23.2% of the successful hijacks we analyze. The attack history thus served both repair and reuse; we derive testable hypotheses for how AI security tools should disclose attacks, such as describing the technique without the full text.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Coherent spin-photon interfaces are essential for scalable quantum networks, but their realization requires optically bright transitions, long-lived spin coherence, and complete coherent control. Donor-bound electron spins in II-VI semiconductors offer an attractive platform for optically active spin qubits because they combine strong donor-bound exciton transitions in a direct-bandgap material with a potentially nuclear-spin-free environment. However, coherent control of an individual optically active donor spin has remained elusive. Here we demonstrate optical initialization, coherent control, and readout of a single donor-bound electron spin in ZnSe. Using spin-selective donor-bound exciton optical transitions, we initialize the electron spin and directly resolve its spin-relaxation dynamics. We achieve coherent spin control with off-resonant picosecond optical pulses, as demonstrated by spin Rabi oscillations and Ramsey interference. We further coherently drive two spin-selective optical transitions and observe high-contrast coherent population trapping, demonstrating the formation of an optically controlled dark state. At higher driving strengths, multiple dark resonances reveal the hyperfine interaction between the electron and the I = 3/2 Cl nucleus. These results establish the first coherent optical control of a single donor electron spin in a II-VI semiconductor and identify isolated optical donors as a promising platform for solid-state optically active qubits.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Traditional multiple sclerosis (MS) image analysis has primarily focused on retrospectively detecting and segmenting lesions. This study investigates whether baseline FLAIR MRI can identify regions at risk for future lesion formation beyond population-level spatial patterns. We introduce FORESEE-MS, an evaluation protocol that uses a fold-specific population-prior atlas as a baseline and assesses predictions using pooled voxel-level discrimination (AUROC and AUPRC) and within-patient lesion localization (Recall@Top-K%), with patient-level bootstrap confidence intervals. We evaluated five deep learning models (3D U-Net, Attn+ResBlock+VAE, ViT, and two SwinUNETR variants) using 5-fold cross-validation on 39 subjects from the MSSEG-2 dataset. The atlas achieved the highest pooled voxel-level AUROC and AUPRC, with no deep learning model reliably outperforming it on either metric. However, the 3D U-Net and Attn+ResBlock+VAE achieved higher mean voxel-level within-patient Recall@Top-K% than the atlas at all evaluated thresholds, although most paired confidence intervals for the differences included zero. These findings suggest that baseline FLAIR may contain patient-specific predictive information, but in this small cohort, it remains uncertain whether this information improves lesion forecasting beyond a population-prior atlas.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
A track fitting pipeline is presented that converts a measured racetrack point cloud into a closed, $C^4$ differentiable, three-dimensional surface model suitable for high-fidelity Modelica race-car optimization. The surface is a Monge patch, parametrised by a curvilinear arc-length coordinate measured along the minimum-curvature line (MCL) and a signed lateral offset, with a height polynomial of user-selectable degree capturing the cross-sectional elevation profile. The choice of MCL as the reference line is deliberate since anchoring the same surface on the geometric centre-line can cause adjacent normals to cross inside the drivable region on tight corners. The resulting non-injective parametrisation assigns multiple curvilinear addresses to the same three-dimensional point and returns invalid road geometry. The MCL is obtained from a quadratic program that minimises integrated curvature subject to track-boundary, periodicity, and jerk-regularisation constraints. By reducing total curvature while remaining within the track bounds, the MCL moves the region of parametrisation breakdown outside the drivable strip on all circuits studied, keeps the normal map injective across the full track width, and yields a more linear time-to-arc-length transformation for minimum lap-time problems. The fitted surface and the associated track widths are exported as periodic piecewise-quintic $C^4$ B-splines, solved as a nonlinear program.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
This paper studies randomised quasi-Monte Carlo (RQMC) methods for Metropolis--Hastings (MH) algorithms, whose accept--reject discontinuity complicates RQMC analysis. To circumvent some of these complications, we study Array-RQMC for MH, with $N$ replicated chains evolved over a fixed time horizon $T$, where we make use of Hilbert sorting for joint multidimensional updates at each step. For one-dimensional MH and bounded-variation test functions, we prove a sampling mean squared error bound of $\mathcal O_T(N^{-4/3})$ relative to the finite-horizon expectation. For product targets, coordinatewise Array-RQMC Metropolis-within-Gibbs retains this exponent for additive marginal bounded-variation tests, with constants that may depend on dimension. With Gaussian random-walk proposals, the bounds extend to scalar and additive marginal polynomials with an additional factor $(\log N)^\ell$, where $\ell$ is the maximum polynomial degree. For joint updates in state dimension $p$ using $p$ proposal uniforms, we provide a conditional $\mathcal O_T(N^{-1-1/(p+2)})$ framework under regularity assumptions that are not verified for the joint multidimensional examples. Numerical experiments support the verified one-dimensional theory and demonstrate variance reduction for joint Hilbert-sorted updates, including Bayesian logistic regression, while illustrating the limitations of these gains as dimension increases.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Homoglyph and invisible-character watermarks are edit-based watermarks. Instead of changing how a model generates text, they hide a signal in the text after it is written. They swap some characters for homoglyphs, which look the same, or very similar, but have different Unicode code points, or they insert characters that do not display, all without access to the model that wrote the text. Generation-time watermarks work less well for lower-resourced languages due to how tokenizers split their text. Because they work on individual characters, these watermarks never touch a tokenizer, so we ask whether they escape this gap. Across 40 language varieties in 24 scripts, we measure capacity (the hidden bits each character can carry), how much of it survives routine handling and targeted removal, and how much text a keyed detector needs. Capacity varies 3.3-fold and script accounts for 96\% of that variation. Within Latin script, resource level makes no detectable difference ($ρ=+0.095$, $p=0.78$), but across scripts capacity rises with it ($ρ=+0.54$, 95\% CI $[+0.14,+0.83]$), because lower-resourced languages tend to use scripts with few homoglyphs. Ordinary copy-paste, which strips invisible characters, widens the gap: a detector then needs about 2 code points of English or Persian but 93 of Lao. Removing the tokenizer does not remove the inequity, but instead only changes its source.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
We study with the semiclassical model the dynamics of a particle moving in a orthorrombic lattice by the hopping mechanism in the presence of a static Coulomb field and a rapidly oscillating homogeneous field. Based on results for the anisotropic Kepler problem, where a chaotic trajectory arises due to different masses of the particle in the X and Y directions, and since this result is also obtained in the rectangular lattice at the continuum limit, the application of the oscillating field allows reparameterizing the effective masses so that they become equal in both directions. Thus, the result is an elliptic trajectory in the continuum limit of the lattice. This chaos-order transition is confirmed by the calculation of Lyapunov exponents for the different trajectories. It is also found that the application of an external magnetic field in the Z direction of the lattice yields chaos control which can be generalized beyond the simple case of the circular trajectory shown in this work. The previous scheme of chaos control was extended for trajectories in 3D in the continuum limit of the orthorrombic lattice which is also equivalent to the far region approximation where the particle moves with respect to the Coulomb field origin. In this case it found that the chaos control technique permits to observe two different dynamical regimes which, although consistent with Bohr-van Leeuwen theorem, suggests that an observable way to distinguish one from the other is to be sought.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Immiscible liquid-liquid jets occur in numerous industrial and environmental settings, including oil spill response and liquid-liquid extraction, yet the coupled evolution of turbulence, interfacial instability, and droplet size distribution across transitional to turbulent regimes remains poorly understood. We present a combined experimental and theoretical investigation of a silicone oil jet injected into refractive-index-matched sugar water, employing simultaneous Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) and Planar Laser-Induced Fluorescence (PLIF). Beyond the breakup region, mean velocity and Reynolds stress profiles exhibit self-similarity. Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) of the volume fraction reveals a systematic shift in the dominant instability mechanism with increasing Reynolds number: axisymmetric Rayleigh-Plateau modes govern breakup at low Reynolds numbers, sinuous and varicose modes coexist in the transitional regime, and Kelvin-Helmholtz-driven shear-layer breakup dominates at higher Reynolds numbers. Droplet sizes are extracted from PLIF images using a convolutional neural network-based segmentation approach. In the transitional regime, a bimodal droplet size distribution is observed, reflecting the coexistence of shear-induced breakup and Rayleigh-Plateau instability. As the Reynolds number increases and turbulent dissipation intensifies, the distribution evolves toward a single mode with smaller characteristic droplet sizes. To predict the droplet size distribution, existing population balance models are extended to include droplet coalescence. Incorporating coalescence substantially improves agreement with experimental measurements, particularly for larger droplets. These findings demonstrate that turbulent dissipation, interfacial instabilities, and droplet coalescence collectively govern the evolution of droplet size distribution in immiscible liquid-liquid jets.

We develop a large-$n$, large-$T$ theory for the unsmoothed fixed-effects quantile regression estimator, paralleling Hahn and Newey (2004) for smooth nonlinear panel models. An exact rank-score identity for the profiled criterion, with a convexity argument, delivers the leading incidental parameter bias of the slope estimator, of order $T^{-1}$, in closed form. When $n$ and $T$ grow at the same rate, the estimator is asymptotically normal but in general not centred, and conventional intervals are invalid. Admissible growth of $n$ relative to $T$, up to $n=o(T^3)$, depends on the regularity of the conditional error densities. A split-panel jackknife removes the leading bias throughout this range and yields valid inference. In serially dependent panels whose dependence decays geometrically or polynomially, the bias acquires a term from the dependence between regressors and errors of different periods, the jackknife remains valid with contiguous but not with interleaved half-panels, and clustered standard errors are valid.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Manifold-valued data arise in a wide range of scientific applications. Existing statistical methods typically follow either an intrinsic approach, which characterizes the manifold itself via quantities such as geodesic distance or the Fréchet mean, or an extrinsic approach, which embeds the manifold into an ambient Euclidean space, performs unconstrained statistical estimation, and projects the result back to the manifold. While the latter is conceptually and computationally simple, likelihood-based extrinsic solutions remain scarce, due to the lack of a general recipe for choosing an embedding map and for characterizing its impact on the transformed distribution. In this article, we tackle the problem using an augmented likelihood approach: we view the manifold-valued data as the Fenchel mirror map of a latent variable, which is nearly unconstrained, and model the latent variable with a canonical distribution, such as Gaussian. The key transform, the Fenchel mirror map, is a generalization of the Euclidean projection and can effectively map into the interior of the manifold. Taking a Bayesian approach, the proposed framework enjoys a generative model interpretation and an augmented likelihood free from intractable normalization constants, and it supports principled uncertainty quantification and flexible model-based extensions. We study the theoretical and computational properties of the framework and demonstrate its utility in analyzing neuroimaging data of high-dimensional correlation time series, where each correlation matrix is rank deficient.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Drone-based 3D reconstruction and inspection require viewpoints that satisfy image-quality constraints while observing each surface region multiple times, which overlap-based planning heuristics do not guarantee. We study ground sample distance (GSD)-constrained $k$-coverage viewpoint selection for structures represented by surface voxels. Candidate viewpoints are generated along outward surface directions, screened with distance, viewing-angle, field-of-view, and occlusion tests, and augmented for voxels with insufficient visibility. Selection is then posed as set multi-cover with per-voxel coverage demands. We propose a dynamically weighted greedy heuristic that prioritizes remaining coverage deficits and scarce viewing alternatives, and compare it with sequential overlap-based pruning and an integer linear programming (ILP) formulation on the same candidate pools. Across two structures, four voxel resolutions, and three coverage requirements, the proposed approach achieves full or near-full $k$-coverage with compact viewpoint sets, using only 3.00--16.39\% more viewpoints than ILP while offering an interpretable selection process based on coverage deficits and viewpoint availability.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
While velocity-commanded RL policies are effective for controlling quadrupeds, they are a limited interface for humanoids that need to perform complex whole-body motions. Furthermore, RL tracking policies for whole-body motions typically have limited information about the desired future motion, preventing them from performing controlled deviations to achieve long-term task success; such information is particularly relevant when a controller must prepare for transitions between behaviors. We address these challenges using concise motion representations that can be generated by a high-level controller, given a behavior label or text command. These representations can be fed directly into a tracking policy to provide a detailed motion reference. Our method exhibits a high degree of flexibility in performing real-world robot motions such as dancing, fighting, or walking based on conditional information. At matched capacity, our adopted stochastic motion tokenizer reconstructs motions from the Unitree G1 at a level that exceeds state-of-the-art approaches such as finite scalar quantization (FSQ) and the vector-quantized autoencoder (VQ-VAE). The resulting discrete interface conditions whole-body tracking policies that execute generated dance, fight, and walk motions lasting 16.8 s each and a 35 s fight-to-dance sequence on a physical Unitree G1.

In this work we discuss their relevance to finite $N$ thermodynamics and the role they play in constraining the partition functions of finite $N$ theories.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Video stylization typically transforms entire scenes, while local artistic editing requires precise region--style association, spatial control, and temporal consistency. We introduce LociArt, a unified paradigm for free-style local video stylization that explicitly specifies where to stylize and what style to apply while preserving non-target content. At its core, GRNStyle builds on Generative Refinement Networks (GRN) and introduces a polar style-aware mask that embeds style identities as equal-norm directions within selected regions. Complementary representation--geometry conditioning combines encoded mask features with raw-mask spatial support, integrating spatiotemporal context with geometric control. To provide paired supervision, we develop an automated pipeline combining global stylization, video object removal, matting, and compositing, and construct the LociArt-100K Dataset with 100K local stylization pairs. We further establish the LociArt Benchmark, comprising 80 source videos and 84 target masks covering 168 foreground/background stylization cases, with a Style Prototype Similarity (SPS) evaluation scheme for regional style quality and complementary measures of non-target preservation and temporal consistency. Experiments show that GRNStyle outperforms existing methods in regional style quality and spatial control while maintaining strong temporal consistency. Qualitative examples further illustrate joint stylization of multiple regions with the same or different learned styles, despite training only on single-region, single-style pairs. Together, these components provide a unified foundation for learning and evaluating controllable local video stylization. Project page: https://higherhu.github.io/lociart/.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Recent long-tailed recognition (LTR) methods incorporate neural collapse (NC) and align features to a fixed Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) as a uniform target for all classes. However, forcing tail classes to fully collapse over-contracts their samples and weakens generalization. To address this, we propose a controlled partial neural collapse, realized through two coordinated controls on a backbone: the Class-Adaptive Sparse Activation (CASA) classifier and the ETF-constrained adaptive margin (ETF-AM) loss. Rather than forcing a uniform full collapse, this regime allows head classes to collapse along the ETF while tail classes retain within-class diversity. This prevents the tail from being forced into full collapse, which is suboptimal under imbalance. To set the dimensionality of collapse, CASA induces class-related node specialization through feature-conditioned gating so that tail classes occupy their own feature directions. For the clearance axis, ETF-AM applies a frequency-adaptive margin, with smaller margins for head classes and larger for tail classes. On CIFAR100-LT, ImageNet-LT, Places-LT, and iNaturalist-2018, our method achieves the best overall accuracy over prior methods. In the empirical analysis, within-class spread increases monotonically from head to tail classes, consistent with tail classes retaining variability rather than fully collapsing.

One dual solution results in the bound \[ S_n\le 2^{n-1} \frac{8n(n-1)(5n-14)} {40n^3-131n^2+4n+136-(5n-14)\lfloor3n/4\rfloor}, \] which improves upon the upper bounds in Lukito, Lukito-van Zanten, and Zémor for $13\le n\le19853$. The second yields the upper bound \[ S_n\le 2^{n-1}\left( 1-\frac1{30\sqrt{3n}}+O(n^{-1}) \right), \] improving upon the asymptotic upper bound of Zémor. Taken together, the two bounds improve upon the upper bounds for $S_n$ in Lukito, Lukito-van Zanten, and Zémor for every $n\ge13$.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
We study 3D visual grounding in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), where a referring expression should identify a target object as both a rendered 2D mask and a set of explicit 3D Gaussians. Prior methods typically extract 3D targets by applying heuristic thresholding or top-ratio filtering to dense primitive-level relevance scores. However, these scores often vary substantially across scenes and prompts, making such heuristics sensitive and leading to unstable targeting. ClusterSplat addresses this by reframing 3D target selection as cluster-level selection over scene-adaptive candidates. The method first learns instance-aware Gaussian features, forms feature-aware seed voxels, and merges neighboring seed voxels when a description-length criterion decreases, producing a scene-specific set of cluster candidates. Given a referring expression, a query-conditioned cluster scorer ranks the cluster candidates with a lightweight MLP, and the selected cluster directly defines the explicit 3D target while its cluster score is rendered for the 2D mask. On ScanRefer, ClusterSplat achieves the best rendered 2D segmentation and explicit 3D target metrics among the compared 3DGS baselines. It also obtains the best average Ref-LERF scores, supporting the same trend under fine-grained referring descriptions. On ScanNet v2 class name queries, ClusterSplat achieves the strongest rendered 2D results and the highest 3D matching accuracy, while maintaining competitive 3D IoU. Our project page is available at https://jaesung8.github.io/clustersplat/ .

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
We establish a uniform effective Chebotarev-Sato-Tate estimate for abelian varieties, conditional on the Mumford-Tate conjecture and the standard analytic conjectures for L-functions attached to the irreducible representations of the Chebotarev-Sato-Tate group. The proof uses spectral majorants and minorants of indicator functions. For regions whose boundaries have finite upper (d-1)-dimensional Minkowski content, the resulting exponent improves that in Bucur et al. (Theorem 1.1, 2024) whenever the Sato-Tate group has rank greater than one. We establish uniform estimates for regions and finite Galois extensions that vary with the counting parameter, and for prime-dependent regions satisfying an explicit variation condition. As an application, we obtain a conditional upper bound for the number of primes at which a weight-two newform with a quadratic coefficient field has a rational Fourier coefficient. We also formulate a discrepancy conjecture, motivated by a probabilistic model, that implies the asymptotic predicted by Murty (Conjecture 3.4, 1999).

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Video models answer from sampled frames and may miss the decisive moment. A common remedy is to commit to an answer, re-examine the video, and confirm or revise it, a loop now mainly learned with reinforcement learning (RL). We find that RL erodes the initial answer, a phenomenon we term confidence erosion, where confidence means the label-verified reliability of the initial answer instead of self-reported certainty: because errors can be repaired later, a correct initial answer earns less reward, and the initial answer stalls even as the final answer's gain over it rises. We propose the principle confident first, reflective second: the initial answer must stay reliable on its own, above a floor set by a reference policy, and reflection may only add to it. Our method, CoFire, implements this principle with one mechanism for each erosion channel: reward incentives, parameter drift, and gradient interference. CoFire reaches 67.0% mean accuracy on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench, 1.7 points above the strongest compared 7B method, and improves initial-answer and final accuracy over outcome-reward RL by 4.1 and 3.7 points on average: a stronger initial answer carries through to a stronger final one.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Kirigami-inspired cuts are an established route to stretchability in two-dimensional materials. At the nanoscale, however, cut edges are not purely geometric: they comprise discrete atomic configurations that can alter the mechanical response. In graphene, a given cut geometry fixes the edge structure; graphyne, a porous carbon allotrope with an intrinsic band gap, lifts this constraint, as identical cut geometries can yield distinct hole-edge configurations. Using molecular dynamics simulations, we report the first atomistic study of $γ$-graphyne kirigami (GYK), and compared with graphene kirigami. GYK reaches yield strains up to 9.6 times that of pristine $γ$-graphyne, with a response governed by both cut geometry and local hole-edge structure. Removing just two carbon atoms at selected edge sites further raises the yield strain by up to 35%, with little loss of yield stress. These findings identify hole-edge atomic configuration as an additional design parameter, expanding the design space for nanoscale kirigami engineering.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
This paper introduces a model for infinite-server queues driven by a Cox process with stochastic intensity given by a squared Bessel (BESQ) process. Exploiting the affine structure of the underlying dynamics, we derive a closed-form expression for the joint moment-generating function (MGF) of the arrival intensity, the number of customers in the system, and the integral of the number of customers in the system over a time interval. This MGF can also be obtained at two (or more) dates, thereby allowing an analysis of the time evolution of infinite-server queues driven by a Cox--BESQ process. The availability of these explicit MGFs enables the development of risk measures for these variables, such as the joint moments of the arrival intensity, the number of customers in the system, and the integral of the number of customers in the system over a time interval, conditional on one of these variables exceeding a critical threshold. These risk measures can be determined at one or two dates. They rely essentially on the explicit form of the MGF of the state variables and on Fourier representations of the risk measures. Numerical experiments demonstrate the practical implementation of the proposed methodology and highlight the relevance of the theoretical results.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Silicon is the dominant platform for integrated photonics, yet its wide electronic bandgap of 1.1 eV fundamentally prevents efficient detection of mid-infrared (MIR) photons through direct valence band to conduction band excitation. Existing approaches therefore seek to enhance sub-bandgap absorption or introduce external infrared absorbers. Here we demonstrate a profoundly different detection strategy based on optically gated transduction, in which MIR photons modulate a pre-established excitation state rather than directly generating photocarriers. Our device integrates Nd3+-doped lanthanide nanoparticles with an inverse-designed Al/p-Si metasurface supporting dual resonances that simultaneously enhances optical gating in the near infrared and resonantly couples incident MIR radiation. The MIR illumination redistributes the Nd3+ emission pathways, producing an optical-state change that is converted into an electrical signal through a silicon Schottky junction. The device achieves room-temperature zero-bias detection at 6.8 um with a modulation responsivity of 103 uA/W and resolves combined gate and MIR inputs into three electrically distinguishable current states. Rather than extending silicon absorption into the infrared, this work establishes gated optical transduction as a route for reading MIR optical information on a silicon platform, opening opportunities for integrated infrared sensing, signal processing and programmable photonic systems.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
The Sinkhorn divergence, a debiased form of entropic optimal transport, has been widely used in various scientific disciplines due to its computational and statistical tractability. Unlike the Wasserstein distance, however, the Sinkhorn divergence is not a metric and it does not naturally admit a formal Riemannian structure. These properties are central to many applications of optimal transport methods that utilize interpolation, barycentric averaging, parallel transport or other geometric operations. Recent work addresses these shortcomings by constructing a formal Riemannian tangent space and a metric tensor on the space of probability measures that quadratically approximates the Sinkhorn divergence. In this work, we extend this framework with two major threads of contributions. For a suitable class of finite-smoothness cost functions, we prove Hadamard differentiability of the Sinkhorn metric tensor and we derive the Levi-Civita covariant derivative in this geometry; we then use the covariant derivative to obtain the geodesic and parallel transport equations, each of which amount to an ODE on a fixed Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) with smooth coefficients. Our second contribution is to linearize the solutions to the geodesic and parallel transport equations using standard tools from Banach space ODE theory. We show that under standard regularity conditions these linearizations imply $\sqrt{n}$-limiting Gaussian processes centered at population values for the plugin estimators of the exponential map, the logarithmic map, parallel transport and the induced Sinkhorn distance. Moreover, we show that the nonparametric bootstrap is consistent for all objects mentioned. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first $\sqrt{n}$--limit theorems and bootstrap consistency results for canonical geometric operations in a transport-based geometry on the space of probability measures.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
We evaluate the archimedean Rankin-Selberg zeta integrals associated with spherical principal series representations of ${\rm SO}_{2n}(\mathbf R) \times {\rm GL}_n(\mathbf R) $ and $ {\rm Sp}_{2n}(\mathbf R) \times {\rm GL}_n(\mathbf R) $, where $ {\rm SO}_{2n} $ is split and $n\ge2$. We obtain explicit formulas expressing these integrals as quotients of products of gamma functions. Our approach uses Mellin-Barnes representations of spherical Whittaker functions, together with new integral identities for their Mellin transforms and transformations of Barnes integrals. In the even orthogonal case, we establish a recurrence in the rank and evaluate the integral by induction. The symplectic case then follows from an explicit identity relating the two families of zeta integrals.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
We present \tool, a query-efficient framework for black-box probabilistic verification. Given a fixed, sampleable input distribution and a binary property oracle, \tool assesses the property's violation probability $p$ against a threshold $θ$. Under independent sampling and stateless oracle behavior, acceptance asserts $p\leθ$, rejection asserts $p>θ+η$ for a user-specified separation margin, and an inconclusive verdict indicates insufficient evidence for either conclusion. The probability of each type of erroneous verdict is bounded by its specified error budget. To support this three-valued contract efficiently, \tool uses a single sequential test, eliminating the interval family required by the baseline. The test accounts for repeated sampling checks through either corrected exact binomial confidence intervals or an anytime-valid confidence sequence. We apply \tool to probabilistic local model semantic consistency, where the property oracle detects decision-level inconsistencies between reference and compiled executions under a specified perturbation distribution. Our evaluation covers 24 tasks across TorchInductor and TensorRT and examines sampling efficiency, conclusiveness, and diagnostic behavior. For sampling efficiency, we use paired one-model clean-label radius searches: the baseline requires 3.6-4.2 times as many unique samples under matched numerical parameters while providing a weaker decision contract. For model semantic consistency, checks at $θ=10^{-3}$ yield 817 acceptances, 19 inconclusive verdicts, and 4 rejections across 840 input--backend instances from 21 tasks. Case studies of two documented compiler faults further demonstrate what these local verdicts can diagnose.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
DNA offers high-density, durable storage by encoding digital information into synthetic strands and retrieving it through sequencing. Sequence reconstruction combines noisy copies of each strand before downstream decoding. Conventional offline methods typically reconstruct completed read clusters, separating reconstruction from ongoing read collection. Streaming reconstruction offers a way to overlap evidence processing with sequencing and reduce the computation remaining before downstream decoding. We present ACOR, a streaming consensus reconstruction method that records $k$-mer transitions and boundary support in a persistent ledger, then decodes through length-constrained beam search and priority-based selection at cluster closure. Evaluation on real and simulated DNA-storage datasets showed competitive recovery. On our own short-read next-generation sequencing (NGS) wet-lab library, ACOR combined near-complete recovery with second-scale reconstruction of more than ten million reads. A smaller public benchmark was completed in a fraction of a second. Parallel ACOR achieved speedups of tens to over a thousand-fold relative to the tested serial baseline configurations. Sparse storage reduced high-context memory requirements, while parallel execution accelerated reconstruction computation. ACOR is designed for streaming readout pipelines that process assigned reads while sequencing continues.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Statistical graphical models are representations of the dependences between the components of a random vector. They encode these dependences via graphical separation criteria. We consider the algorithmic problem of checking separation statements for the various graph classes and separation criteria that have been developed by the community. We establish that all criteria we study can be checked by modular variations of reachability. For all separation criteria but $σ$-separation, this yields a linear-time algorithm. This is effectively the optimal attainable time since loading the graph itself is linear-time in the number of edges in the graph. Using the CIfly framework for deploying modular variations of reachability, we also provide R and Python code implementing our algorithms. We evaluate empirical runtime and scaling behavior in a simulation study.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) provide reusable whole-body motion priors: given a kinematic reference, they generate coordinated joint commands for motion replay, teleoperation, and VLA control. However, trained primarily on flat-ground motion, BFMs lack an explicit mechanism to adapt foot placement, swing clearance, and contact timing to local terrain. Many terrain-aware BFM approaches address this limitation by retraining or fine-tuning the tracker together with perception, incurring substantial data and computation costs while coupling ordinary tracking to the perception pathway. To bridge this gap, we propose GRAFT, a geometry-aware residual adaptation framework for frozen behavior trackers. GRAFT preserves the BFM parameters and motion-reference interface, while a lightweight adapter adds terrain-conditioned corrections only to lower-body execution targets. The adapter is trained with task and foot-geometry rewards, regularized to suppress unnecessary corrections on flat ground, and distilled from privileged terrain observations to onboard depth. Because the frozen BFM already provides whole-body reference tracking and nominal locomotion, GRAFT reduces terrain learning to a focused execution-adaptation problem. We instantiate the framework on four frozen trackers and evaluate stairs, gaps, and platforms in simulation. We further validate it through real-world deployment on a Unitree G1, where the adapted SONIC tracker traverses terrain with onboard depth and unmodified references.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Agentic life-science benchmarks give an agent evidence about a named entity and score an answer against a recorded outcome. That score tests reasoning over evidence only if the evidence, rather than the name, determines the answer. We examine this distinction by varying identity and evidence independently on a clinical-outcome benchmark and published tasks from Biomni and LAB-Bench. Blinding identity matters little when a prompt contains a decisive sequence or passage. It matters a great deal when the prompt is mostly a name and candidate list (0.742 named versus 0.082 blinded; chance 0.093). Across 96 LAB-Bench LitQA2 questions, the gap increases under one fixed passage-redaction scheme (+0.000 to +0.135; per-instance slope +0.147, p= 0.004). On the clinical benchmark, a no-evidence recall probe matches prediction accuracy and recovers a database-specific programme count. So, we argue that benchmarks intended to measure evidence-dependent reasoning should report identity-blinded results, retrieval telemetry, and positive controls.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
A major challenge facing AI scientific discovery pipelines is how to determine when a generated idea is meaningfully novel. Ideally, novelty checks in these pipelines must be able to reject non-novel ideas while not rejecting too many novel ideas, and they should also be able to distinguish which parts of a proposal are non-novel, as opposed to opaquely discarding entire proposals. We design an analytical framework for evaluation of novelty checks with temporal ground truth at both the proposal- and claim-level, using four datasets of 1,060 proposals built from published papers, reviewer disputes, and generated ideas matching ones the field went on to publish. Auditing existing novelty checks with this framework, we find that checks with high rejection rates on non-novel work also tend to have high false alarms on ideas that are later realized by human researchers, and observe that checks built to evaluate proposals as a whole can point to claim-level prior art only by rejecting the whole proposal. We therefore introduce ClaimNov, a fine-grained, interpretable claim-level novelty module. ClaimNov catches 97% of disguised papers at a 1.5% false-alarm rate, and its claim-level novelty profile cuts the LLM judge's false alarms from 11.8% to 1.5%. Because its verdict rests on claim-level evidence, ClaimNov also keeps proposals that build on established contributions, rejecting only 3% of ICLR-accepted proposals with a reviewer-disputed contribution and keeping 91 of 100 novel proposals with one spliced prior contribution, against 76 for the strongest existing check. Code and data are available at https://github.com/emmatliu/claimnov.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Odd radio circles (ORCs) are a recently recognized class of faint, roughly circular diffuse radio sources, typically a few hundred kiloparsecs across, whose origin is still debated. We report the serendipitous discovery of a giant ORC, ORC~J1928$-$5056, in 856~MHz continuum data from the ASKAP observations. The emission forms a single, mildly elliptical structure $4^{\prime}$ across, corresponding to $0.63$~Mpc at the redshift $z=0.1507$ of the central galaxy LEDA~140850, the brightest cluster galaxy of Abell~3639, which makes it one of the largest single ORCs known. After subtracting the radio nucleus associated with the host galaxy, the ORC has a flux density of 73~mJy integrated within an area of $\sim 12$~arcmin$^2$, i.e.\ a mean surface brightness of only $1.7$~$μ$Jy~arcsec$^{-2}$, and a rest-frame luminosity of $L_{1.4}=2\times10^{24}$~W~Hz$^{-1}$, comparable to those of the most luminous ORCs. Including its nucleus, the system reaches $L_{1.4}=6.6\times10^{24}$~W~Hz$^{-1}$, higher than that of any other ORC reported so far. The host is a massive ($M_{\ast}\sim10^{11}\,M_{\odot}$), passive elliptical galaxy with negligible star formation. It contains an AGN jet with a power-law spectrum of index $α=-0.877\pm0.089$ between 856 and 1656~MHz. Finally, we discuss the implications for ORC formation models and the observations needed to establish the nature of this system.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Learned flow surrogates are applied recursively, so errors in phase, amplitude and transport accumulate as each prediction feeds the next. During training, however, the realized next state is known. We propose Future-Aligned Motion Inference for Recursive Physical Forecasting (FAMIR), which uses this realized future to shape the signal that drives the update, not only the predicted state. On the latent grid of a frozen autoencoder, a future-conditioned teacher and a history-only student infer motion tensors that condition one shared residual transition. Posterior--Prior Motion Alignment (PPMA) jointly aligns the teacher (posterior) and student (prior) motions, prediction-fed multistep objectives train the student on its own rollouts, and only the student is deployed. On viscoelastic channel flow, Rayleigh--Bénard convection and planetary shallow-water flow, FAMIR achieves lower complete-prefix normalized root-mean-square error than three direct latent predictors of comparable size and a delay-embedded linear reference at ten steps (1.003\%, 1.055%, 0.620%) and twenty steps (1.661%, 1.683%, 1.036%). Its advantage is largest at the first step in the viscoelastic flow and grows with lead time in the other flows. Over forty-step forecasts, FAMIR keeps fluctuation profiles and probability densities closer to the reference than the direct predictors. Without the teacher, the motion-conditioned student already outperforms the direct predictors; in the shallow-water flow, prediction-fed rollouts are decisive and joint alignment is far more effective than distillation toward a fixed teacher (1.036% against 1.874%). Fixed-state interventions show that the trained update relies on the state-specific motion, and the deployed student matches the one-step accuracy of the future-informed teacher.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
We study a finite-state mean-field game with entropic control cost. In the large population limit, we show that its stationary Nash equilibria satisfy the detailed balance condition and their distributions take the Gibbsian form with the value function playing the role of a Hamiltonian. We apply the entropic control cost to a ferromagnetic mean-field Ising game and investigate its stationary and non-stationary Nash equilibria. We find that the stationary Nash equilibria exhibit a second-order phase transition from disordered to ordered equilibria as temperature decreases. A center-manifold reduction yields non-stationary Nash equilibrium near the critical temperature and reveals the critical slowing down in the relaxation toward the stationary Nash equilibrium.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Motivation: PERMANOVA is widely used to test associations between covariates and high-dimensional data with arbitrary distributions, such as ecology, metabolomics, or microbial community profiling. In these contexts, its effect size measure (R2) is generally used to indicate how much the high-dimensional measurement covaries with respect to a separate, univariate measure. However, as we show, this conventional effect size is inflated under the null, resulting in values that do not accurately reflect the conventional expectation of "variance explained." Furthermore, standard permutation schemes yield inflated false positives in the presence of non-independent samples, such as repeated measure designs. Results: We introduce confounding-aware permutation schemes for both invariant and variant covariates. We additionally develop a causally-grounded, distance-based effect-size estimator derived from the Hájek average treatment effect estimator, providing interpretable effect sizes in the units of the chosen dissimilarity metric. Simulations using microbiome profiles demonstrate that these approaches control false positives while maintaining power, outperforming standard PERMANOVA implementations. Availability and Implementation: An R implementation is freely available in the permaBrioche module of the bioBakery ecosystem https://huttenhower.sph.harvard.edu/permabrioche. Contact: chuttenh@hsph.harvard.edu

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Fisher zero lines of the Loschmidt amplitude in non-Hermitian quenches can exhibit anomalous structures in the complex time plane, such as divergence, separation, and the restriction of all branches or a specific branch to the real or imaginary axis. Here, we use the biorthogonal framework to reveal the origin of these structures and determine the corresponding critical momentum conditions by analyzing the values of $m_k=\hat{\mathbf{h}}_0\cdot\hat{\mathbf{h}}_1$, the dot product between the normalized prequench and postquench complex Bloch vectors. When Fisher zeros continuously cover the real-time axis, the density of Fisher zeros is further introduced to identify the critical times within these critical regions, at which the rate function becomes nonanalytic. We verify our results in a generalized non-Hermitian SSH model by quenching the Peierls phase and the non-Hermitian gain-loss strength, and also use the Jordan form to analyze the dynamics at postquench exceptional points, where the conventional Fisher zero formula is not applicable.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
The Ramsey number $R(G_1,G_2)$ is the smallest positive integer $n$ such that for every graph $H$ on $n$ vertices, either $H$ contains a copy of $G_1$ or the complement $\overline H$ contains a copy of $G_2$. Ramsey numbers involving the book graphs $B_n$, which consist of $n$ triangles sharing a common edge, have attracted recent attention, especially in the ``nearly diagonal'' case $R(B_{n-1},B_n)$. Rousseau and Sheehan showed the upper bound $R(B_{n-1},B_n) \le 4n-1$ nearly fifty years ago, but no general matching lower bound construction is known. This paper gives several new infinite families of $n$ for which $R(B_{n-1},B_n) = 4n-1$. Some of the main results in this paper were found with assistance from the Station, a multi-agent AI system. These results also appeared in a larger work on autonomous mathematical discovery by the authors and Du in arxiv:2608.23691. This paper is a follow-up to that work: we give complete proofs of the book Ramsey results and discuss their connections to objects in combinatorial design theory.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
As agents collaborate on longer tasks, responsibility may pass between models before the work is complete. The receiving model must build on prior decisions, observations, and actions while addressing the remaining requirements. Evaluating this transition requires connecting the information preserved at handoff to how the receiver continues the work, a relationship that task-success and memory-retention scores alone do not capture. We introduce the Handoff State Continuity Benchmark (HSC-Bench), comprising 1,039 tasks that evaluate two complementary aspects of task takeover: recovering relevant repository evidence and continuing from established conversational, tool, and file-work state. Comparisons across six receiving models show that structured handoff state improves repository evidence recovery for every model and continuation performance for most models. The strongest receivers differ between the two tracks, showing that evidence-recovery rankings alone do not characterize performance when continuing from inherited state. By combining these comparisons with checks of subsequent responses and actions, HSC-Bench evaluates both access to prior evidence and adherence to established commitments and completed work. This provides a basis for selecting receiving models and assessing handoff representations according to the work that must be carried forward.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
We study the minimum number of orthogonal projective measurement settings needed to estimate multiple observables without bias for arbitrary input states. We derive structural bounds that go beyond dimension counting and combine them with explicit constructions to certify minimum setting counts for selected target spaces. A classical variational algorithm searches for shared measurement bases and optimizes their readout coefficients and sample allocation. For the collective first and second moments of two qubits, we certify that four projective settings are necessary and sufficient. For this task, a numerically optimized four-setting design achieves a Haar-averaged variance within approximately $0.0341\%$ of a lower bound valid for any number of projective settings in our fixed-allocation, unbiased linear estimation model. Numerical examples show that shared measurements can improve precision relative to the comparison protocols. For finite-depth circuits, we account for reconstruction bias and identify finite-sample regimes in which this advantage persists.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Distribution logistics with capacity constraints and service priorities can be modeled as a variant of the \emph{TSP with Profits} (TSPP), in which not all customers need to be visited and the selection of which customers to serve is part of the problem. This paper proposes an applied variant with two adaptations: (i) a 0/1 Knapsack objective function weighted by client priority squared ($v_i \cdot p_i^2$), and (ii) a priority bias in the Nearest Neighbor heuristic for the TSP, parameterized by $α$. The approach is evaluated on a scenario with 14 customers and a 1,100~kg capacity, complemented by a comparative experimental protocol against the classical greedy heuristic ($v_i/w_i$ ordering) and an integer programming solver. Results on the base scenario show 9 customers served, 96.4\% capacity utilization, and R\$~18,392.60 revenue, with all 5 excluded customers being low-priority. A sensitivity analysis of the priority exponent justifies the quadratic choice. The limitations of the hierarchical decomposition are explicitly discussed.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Written transcripts of the same speech can differ in ways that are not uniquely determined by the speech signal. We formulate evaluation-side transcript canonicalization (ETC), which maps multiple surface forms to a single canonical form when their differences are not determined by speech. To our knowledge, ETC-Bench is the first and most comprehensive multilingual benchmark for evaluation-side transcript canonicalization, covering 181 phenomenon types across 12 languages. Each instance is a minimal pair that shares a sentence context and differs only in a target span exhibiting one phenomenon. To evaluate both canonicalization success and semantic preservation, we propose Semantic-preserving Exact-match Normalization Accuracy (SENA), which combines exact agreement between independently canonicalized pair members with a pair-relative BERTScore constraint against information loss. We further introduce the Taxonomy-guided Agent Canonicalization Skill (TACS), which provides LLM agents with phenomenon descriptions and explicit canonicalization contracts. Experiments with five baseline configurations and three TACS-based agents show that the agents outperform the baseline systems on shared languages. ETC-Bench provides a systematic testbed for evaluation-side transcript canonicalization across languages.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
We study completely normal elements of $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$, that is, elements that are normal over every intermediate field, through partial Lagrange resolvents. In these coordinates, complete normality splits into independent components, in a way closely related to Hachenberger's decomposition theory. Our main tool is a structure theorem for the components; together with a finite computation, it shows that every component has weight (the sum of the probabilities that its conditions fail) at most $3/4$, uniformly in $n$. Combined with the classical character-sum method, this gives an explicit sufficient criterion for the existence of a primitive completely normal element. We verify the criterion for all $n>q$ except $70$ pairs $(q,n)$, which we settle with explicit elements found by computer. Since the case $n\le q$ is due to Garefalakis and Kapetanakis, this confirms the conjecture of Morgan and Mullen (1996) that every $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ contains a primitive element that is completely normal over $\mathbb{F}_q$. The same estimates give two further results. First, Hachenberger's conjectured lower bound $(q-1)^{n'}q^{(p^a-1)n'}$ for the number of completely normal elements, where $p$ is the characteristic and $n=p^an'$ with $p\nmid n'$, holds for all pairs $(q,n)$; it was known for regular pairs. Second, primitivity and complete normality are asymptotically independent: as $q^n\to\infty$, the number of primitive completely normal elements is $(1+o(1))\,\varphi(q^n-1)/(q^n-1)$ times the number of completely normal elements (for fixed $n$ this was known). Our arguments for $n>q$ and for both further results, including every computer-assisted step, are formalised in Lean 4 with Mathlib; the formalisation takes the case $n\le q$ and an explicit bound of Rosser and Schoenfeld as axioms and relies on Lean's compiler and interpreter for the large computations.

Abstract of a paper posted to arXiv:
Differences in musculoskeletal morphology challenge policy reuse across individual models. Here we present MyoAcross, a framework that combines individual musculoskeletal model construction, morphology-conditioned policy learning and virtual model augmentation to enable muscle-driven reference-motion tracking without individual fine-tuning. Across 31 held-out individual models, MyoAcross achieves 99.24% completion and reduces tracking error by 22.60% relative to an unconditioned multilayer perceptron. Policy reuse extends to models of 22 held-out individuals constructed from single-image shape estimates, measured height and body mass, and, with asymmetry augmentation, to models with unilateral lower-limb shortening. Comparisons with measurements from 120 additional individuals show agreement in vertical ground reaction force waveforms and channel-dependent agreement between simulated muscle activations and electromyography. These results establish a common control framework for comparative simulations of movement across individual musculoskeletal models.
